chapters.title: Prelude
paragraphs: Who, if they care deeply about human history and the behaviour of that mysterious mixture under Time's changing experiments, has not paused, at least briefly, over the life of Saint Theresa? Who has not smiled tenderly at the thought of the little girl setting off one morning, hand in hand with her even smaller brother, to seek martyrdom in the land of the Moors? They toddled out of rugged Avila, as wide-eyed and apparently helpless as two fawns, yet with human hearts already beating to a national ideal, until the realities of home, in the shape of their uncles, intercepted them and turned them back from their great purpose. That childhood pilgrimage was a fitting beginning. Theresa's passionate, idealistic nature demanded an epic life: what could the many volumes of chivalric romances, or a brilliant girl's triumphs in society, mean to her? Her fire soon consumed such flimsy fuel. Sustained from within, it rose towards some boundless satisfaction, some purpose that could never excuse weariness, that would reconcile despair of herself with the ecstatic awareness of a life beyond herself. She found her epic in reforming a religious order.

That Spanish woman, who lived three hundred years ago, was certainly not the last of her kind. Many Theresas have been born without finding an epic life in which great actions unfolded continuously and sent their echoes far away. They may have found only a life of mistakes, born of a certain greatness of spirit poorly matched with the smallness of their opportunities; perhaps a tragic failure that found no sacred poet and slipped, unmourned, into oblivion. With little light to guide them and circumstances tangled around them, they tried to bring their thoughts and actions into noble harmony. Yet to ordinary eyes their struggles seemed nothing but inconsistency and shapelessness. These later Theresas had no coherent social faith or order to supply the place of knowledge for the soul passionately willing to act. Their fervour shifted between a vague ideal and the ordinary longings of womanhood: the first was censured as extravagance, the second condemned as a falling away.

Some have thought these stumbling lives the result of the inconvenient lack of definition with which the Supreme Power has made women's natures. If female incompetence had one fixed level, as definite as the ability to count to three and no further, women's place in society could be settled with scientific certainty. The indefiniteness persists, however, and the actual range of variation is far wider than anyone would guess from the uniformity of women's hairstyles and their favourite love stories in prose and verse. Here and there a young swan grows up uneasily among the ducklings in a brown pond and never finds the flowing stream and the company of its own paddle-footed kind. Here and there a Saint Theresa is born who founds nothing, whose loving heartbeats and sobs for a goodness never reached tremble away and scatter among obstacles, instead of gathering into some deed that people will recognize long afterwards.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter I
paragraphs:
Since being a woman keeps me from doing good,
Let me keep reaching for what comes closest to it.
—_The Maid’s Tragedy:_ BEAUMONT AND FLETCHER.

Miss Brooke had the kind of beauty that plain clothing seems to bring out. Her hand and wrist were so finely shaped that she could wear sleeves as innocent of fashion as those in which Italian painters clothed the Blessed Virgin. Her profile, height and bearing all seemed to gain dignity from her simple clothes. Among the fashions of the provinces, they gave her the force of a fine quotation from the Bible—or from one of our older poets—set into a paragraph of today's newspaper. People generally called her remarkably clever, though they added that her sister Celia had more common sense. Yet Celia wore hardly any more ornament. Only a close observer could see the difference between her clothes and her sister's, and the faint touch of coquetry in their arrangement. Miss Brooke dressed plainly for a combination of reasons, most of which also applied to her sister. Pride in being ladies had something to do with it: the Brookes' connections, though not precisely aristocratic, were unquestionably “good.” Look back a generation or two and you would find no ancestors measuring cloth by the yard or tying parcels—no one below an admiral or a clergyman. There was even an identifiable Puritan gentleman who had served under Cromwell, later conformed to the established church, and emerged from all the political turmoil still owning a respectable family estate. Young women of this birth, living in a quiet country house and attending a village church scarcely bigger than a drawing room, naturally thought finery an ambition for a small trader's daughter. There was also genteel thrift, which in those days made extravagant clothing the first expense to cut whenever money was needed for spending that better distinguished one's rank. These reasons alone would have explained plain dress, without any religious feeling. In Miss Brooke's case, however, religion by itself would have settled the matter. Celia gently accepted all her sister's views, merely tempering them with the common sense that can take in momentous doctrines without any peculiar disturbance. Dorothea knew many passages of Pascal's Pensees and Jeremy Taylor by heart. To her, human destiny viewed in the light of Christianity made the worries of women's fashion seem an occupation for Bedlam. She could not reconcile the concerns of a spiritual life, with their eternal consequences, and a lively interest in ornamental braid and artificially puffed-out skirts. Her mind dealt in theories and naturally yearned for some exalted view of the world that could openly take in the parish of Tipton and her own conduct there. Intensity and greatness enchanted her, and she recklessly embraced anything that seemed to possess them. She was likely to seek martyrdom, to retract her beliefs, and then to suffer martyrdom after all in some unexpected place. Such traits in a marriageable girl were certainly apt to complicate her future, preventing it from being settled in the customary way by beauty, vanity and a merely doglike affection. For all this, she was not yet twenty, though the older sister. Since losing their parents at about twelve, both girls had been educated by arrangements at once restrictive and haphazard, first in an English family and then in a Swiss one at Lausanne. Their unmarried uncle and guardian had hoped in this way to make up for the disadvantages of being orphans.

Scarcely a year had passed since they came to live with their uncle at Tipton Grange. Nearly sixty, he was an agreeable man of assorted opinions and unpredictable voting habits. He had travelled when young, and in this part of the county people thought his mind had acquired too great a habit of wandering. Mr. Brooke's conclusions were as hard to forecast as the weather. All one could safely say was that his intentions would be kindly, and that he would spend as little as possible in putting them into practice. Even the stickiest, vaguest minds contain a few hard grains of habit. A man may be careless about every interest of his own except keeping hold of his snuffbox, which he watches suspiciously and clutches with greed.

In Mr. Brooke the inherited strain of Puritan energy was plainly dormant. In his niece Dorothea it shone through virtues and faults alike, sometimes becoming impatience with her uncle's conversation or his habit of “letting things be” on the estate. It made her long all the more to come of age and control some money for generous projects. People considered her an heiress. Besides the seven hundred pounds a year each sister had from their parents, if Dorothea married and bore a son he would inherit Mr. Brooke's estate, thought to bring in about three thousand a year. Such a rental looked like wealth to provincial families still discussing Mr. Peel's recent conduct on the Catholic question, unaware of the goldfields to come and of that splendid plutocracy which has so nobly raised the cost of a genteel existence.

And how could Dorothea fail to marry—a girl so beautiful, with such prospects? Only her taste for extremes could prevent it, and her determination to arrange life by ideas that might make a cautious man hesitate before proposing, or might even make her reject every proposal. A young woman of family and fortune who would suddenly kneel on a brick floor beside a sick labourer and pray fervently as though she lived in the days of the Apostles—who had strange fancies for fasting like a Papist and staying up at night over old theological books! A wife like that might wake you one fine morning with a new plan for spending her income that interfered with political economy and the keeping of riding horses. Naturally a man would think twice before risking such a partnership. Women were expected to have unsound opinions; the great protection of society and the home was that nobody acted on them. Sensible people did what their neighbours did, so that any lunatics wandering free could be recognized and avoided.

Country opinion of the new young ladies, even among the cottage dwellers, generally preferred Celia, who looked so sweet-tempered and innocent. Miss Brooke's great eyes seemed, like her religion, too unusual and arresting. Poor Dorothea! Beside her, innocent-looking Celia was knowing and worldly: the human mind is so much subtler than the outer tissues that serve as its coat of arms or clock face.

Yet people who met Dorothea, even when this alarming gossip had prejudiced them, discovered a charm that somehow coexisted with everything they had heard. Most men found her enchanting on horseback. She loved the open air and the countryside's changing appearances, and when combined pleasures lit up her eyes and cheeks, she looked very little like a religious devotee. Riding was an indulgence she permitted herself despite her uneasy conscience. She felt she enjoyed it with a pagan delight in the senses, and always anticipated giving it up.

She was candid, passionate and entirely without self-admiration. It was charming, indeed, to see how her imagination gave her sister Celia attractions far beyond her own. If any gentleman seemed to visit the Grange for a reason other than seeing Mr. Brooke, she concluded that he must love Celia. Sir James Chettam, for example, she always considered from Celia's perspective, privately weighing whether accepting him would be good for her sister. The idea that anyone could regard him as her own suitor would have struck her as absurdly beside the point. Despite her eagerness to discover life's truths, Dorothea's ideas about marriage remained very childish. She was sure she would have accepted the judicious Hooker, had she been born in time to save him from his miserable marital mistake; or John Milton once he went blind; or any of those other great men whose odd habits it would have been gloriously devout to endure. But a pleasant, handsome baronet who answered “Exactly” even when her remarks expressed uncertainty—how could he move her as a lover? A truly delightful marriage must be one in which your husband was something like a father and could even teach you Hebrew, if you wanted.

These peculiarities in Dorothea made neighbouring families blame Mr. Brooke all the more for failing to find a middle-aged lady to guide and accompany his nieces. But he so dreaded the kind of superior woman likely to be available for the post that he let Dorothea's objections dissuade him. On this matter he was brave enough to defy the world—meaning Mrs. Cadwallader, the Rector's wife, and the little circle of gentry with whom he exchanged visits in north-east Loamshire. So Miss Brooke ran her uncle's household, and was by no means displeased with her new authority and the deference that went with it.

Today Sir James Chettam was to dine at the Grange with another gentleman the girls had never met, whose arrival Dorothea anticipated with a certain reverence. He was the Reverend Edward Casaubon, known throughout the county for profound learning and understood to have spent many years on a great work of religious history. He also possessed enough wealth to lend his piety lustre, and opinions of his own that would become clearer when his book appeared. His very name had an impressive weight which could hardly be measured without a precise chronology of scholarship.

Earlier that day Dorothea had returned from the infant school she had established in the village. She was settling into her usual place in the pretty sitting room between the sisters' bedrooms, intent on finishing a plan for some buildings—a kind of work she loved—when Celia, who had been watching her and hesitating over a suggestion, said—

“Dorothea, dear, if you don't mind—if you aren't too busy—could we look at mamma's jewels today and divide them? It's exactly six months today since uncle gave them to you, and you haven't even looked at them.”

A trace of a pout shadowed Celia's face. Her habitual awe of Dorothea and principle held the full pout back: these two connected powers could give a mysterious electric shock if carelessly touched. To her relief, Dorothea looked up with laughter in her eyes.
“What a marvellous little almanac you are, Celia! Do you mean six calendar months or six lunar ones?”

“Today is the last day of September, and uncle gave them to you on the first of April. You remember he said he'd forgotten them until then. I don't believe you've thought of them since you locked them in this cabinet.”
“Well, dear, you know we'd never wear them.” Dorothea's voice was warm and affectionate, half a caress and half an explanation. Pencil in hand, she was sketching little side plans in a margin.

Celia flushed and looked very serious. “I think, dear, we're being disrespectful to mamma's memory by putting them away and taking no notice of them. Besides,” she added after a little hesitation, a sob of hurt rising in her voice, “necklaces are quite usual now. Madame Poincon, who was even stricter than you about some things, used to wear ornaments. And Christians in general—surely there are women in heaven now who wore jewels.” When Celia really gave her mind to arguing, she felt she had some intellectual strength.

“You'd like to wear them?” Dorothea exclaimed. Astonished discovery animated her whole body with a theatrical movement learned from that same ornament-wearing Madame Poincon. “Well, of course, let's get them out. Why didn't you tell me before? But the keys, the keys!” She pressed her hands to the sides of her head, apparently despairing of her memory.
“Here they are,” said Celia, who had long thought out and prepared for this conversation.
“Please open the cabinet's large drawer and take out the jewel box.”

Soon the open box stood before them and the jewels lay spread across the table like a bright flower bed. The collection was small, but some pieces were remarkably beautiful. The finest immediately visible were a necklace of purple amethysts in delicate gold settings, and a pearl cross set with five brilliant-cut diamonds. Dorothea picked up the necklace at once and fastened it round her sister's neck, where it fitted nearly as tightly as a bracelet. The circle suited the Henrietta-Maria style of Celia's head and neck, though, as she could see for herself in the tall mirror opposite.
“There, Celia! That will go with your Indian muslin. But you must wear this cross with your dark dresses.”
Celia struggled to keep from smiling with delight. “Oh, Dodo, you must keep the cross for yourself.”
“No, no, dear, no,” Dorothea answered, raising her hand in a casual gesture of refusal.
“Yes, you really must. It would look well on you—with your black dress, for instance,” Celia insisted. “Surely you _could_ wear that.”
“Not for anything, not for anything. A cross is the very last thing I'd wear as a bauble.” Dorothea gave a slight shudder.
“Then you'll think it wicked of me to wear it,” Celia said uneasily.
“No, dear, no,” Dorothea said, stroking her sister's cheek. “Souls have their own complexions too. What suits one won't suit another.”
“But perhaps you'd like to keep it in memory of mamma.”
“No, I have other things of mamma's—her sandalwood box that I love so much—plenty of things. Really, they're all yours, dear. There's no need to discuss it any longer. There—take your property away.”
Celia felt rather hurt. This Puritan tolerance assumed a strong superiority, scarcely easier for the fair flesh of an unenthusiastic sister to bear than Puritan persecution.
“But how can I wear jewellery when you, my older sister, won't ever wear any?”

“Really, Celia, it's too much to ask me to put on trinkets just to make you feel comfortable. Wearing a necklace like that would make me feel as though I'd been spinning round on my toes. The world would whirl about me, and I wouldn't know how to walk.”

Celia had undone the necklace and taken it off. “It would be a little tight round your neck. Something that lay lower and hung down would suit you better,” she said with some satisfaction. The necklace's complete unsuitability for Dorothea, from every point of view, made Celia happier to accept it. She was opening some ring boxes, revealing a fine emerald surrounded by diamonds, when the sun emerged from behind a cloud and cast a bright gleam across the table.

“How beautiful these stones are!” Dorothea said, swept by a new feeling as sudden as the sunlight. “It's strange how deeply colours seem to enter us, like a scent. I suppose that's why jewels serve as spiritual symbols in the Revelation of St. John. They look like pieces of heaven. I think that emerald is the most beautiful of all.”
“There's a bracelet to match,” Celia said. “We didn't notice this one at first.”

“They're lovely,” said Dorothea, slipping the ring and bracelet onto her delicately shaped finger and wrist and raising them towards the window at eye level. All the time her mind was trying to justify her delight in their colours by blending it with her mystical religious joy.

“You _would_ like those, Dorothea,” Celia said with some hesitation, beginning to wonder at this sign of weakness in her sister. She also thought emeralds would suit her own colouring even better than purple amethysts. “You must keep the ring and bracelet, if you keep nothing else. But look, these agates are very pretty and unobtrusive.”

“Yes! I'll keep these—the ring and bracelet,” Dorothea said. Then she lowered her hand to the table and spoke in a different tone. “Yet what wretched men must find these things, and work on them, and sell them!” She paused again. Celia thought her sister was about to give up the jewels, as consistency surely required.
“Yes, dear, I will keep these,” Dorothea said firmly. “But take everything else away, and the box as well.”
She picked up her pencil, still wearing the jewels and still looking at them. She imagined often keeping them nearby, nourishing her eyes at these little springs of pure colour.
“Will you wear them when we have company?” Celia asked, watching with genuine curiosity about what her sister would do.

Dorothea shot her sister a glance. Through all the imaginative beauty with which she clothed the people she loved, a sharp perception sometimes flashed, and it could scorch. If Miss Brooke ever achieved perfect meekness, it would not be because she lacked an inward fire.
“Perhaps,” she replied rather loftily. “I can't say how low I may sink.”

Celia blushed and felt miserable. She knew she had offended her sister, and did not dare even to say something grateful about the jewellery as she returned it to its box and carried it away. Dorothea was unhappy too. Continuing with her architectural plans, she questioned the purity of her feelings and words during the scene that had ended in that little outburst.

Celia's own conscience assured her she had done nothing wrong. Her question had been perfectly natural and reasonable, and she kept telling herself Dorothea was inconsistent. Either she should have taken her full share of the jewels or, after saying what she had, refused them altogether.

“I'm sure—or at least I hope,” Celia thought, “that wearing a necklace won't interfere with my prayers. And I can't see why Dorothea's opinions should bind me now we're going into society, though of course they ought to bind her. But Dorothea isn't always consistent.”
So Celia reflected, silently bending over her embroidery, until she heard her sister call.
“Here, Kitty, come and look at my plan. I'll think myself a great architect if I haven't put the stairs and fireplaces where they clash.”

As Celia bent over the sheet, Dorothea affectionately pressed her cheek against her sister's arm. Celia understood. Dorothea recognized she had been wrong, and Celia forgave her. For as long as either could remember, Celia had regarded her older sister with a mixture of criticism and awe. The younger had always worn a yoke. But is there any creature under a yoke that has no private opinions?

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter II
paragraphs:
“‘Dime; no ves aquel caballero que hacia nosotros viene sobre un
caballo rucio rodado que trae puesto en la cabeza un yelmo de oro?’ ‘Lo
que veo y columbro,’ respondio Sancho, ‘no es sino un hombre sobre un
as no pardo como el mio, que trae sobre la cabeza una cosa que
relumbra.’ ‘Pues ese es el yelmo de Mambrino,’ dijo Don
Quijote.”—CERVANTES.

“‘Don't you see that knight coming towards us on a dapple-grey horse, wearing a golden helmet?’ ‘All I can see,’ Sancho answered, ‘is a man on a grey donkey like mine, with something shiny on his head.’ ‘Precisely,’ Don Quixote replied, ‘and that shining object is the helmet of Mambrino.’”

“Sir Humphry Davy?” said Mr. Brooke over the soup, smiling in his easy way as he picked up Sir James Chettam's remark about studying Davy's Agricultural Chemistry. “Well, now, Sir Humphry Davy. I dined with him years ago at Cartwright's, and Wordsworth was there too—the poet Wordsworth, you know. There's a curious thing. I was at Cambridge at the same time as Wordsworth and never met him, and twenty years later I dined with him at Cartwright's. Things do turn out oddly. But Davy was there; he was a poet as well. Or you might say Wordsworth was poet number one, and Davy poet number two. True in every sense, you know.”

Dorothea felt rather more uneasy than usual. At the start of dinner, with so few people and such a quiet room, these specks shaken from the bulk of a magistrate's mind fell too conspicuously. How, she wondered, could a man like Mr. Casaubon bear such trivial conversation? His manner seemed very dignified to her. The arrangement of his iron-grey hair and his deep-set eyes reminded her of Locke's portrait. He had the lean figure and pale complexion appropriate to a scholar, utterly unlike the flourishing, red-whiskered English type embodied by Sir James Chettam.

“I'm reading Agricultural Chemistry,” said that excellent baronet, “because I intend to manage one of the farms myself and see whether I can set my tenants a good example of farming. Do you approve, Miss Brooke?”

“A great mistake, Chettam,” Mr. Brooke broke in. “Electrifying your land and that sort of thing, turning your cowshed into a drawing room. It won't do. I went deeply into science myself at one time, but I saw it wouldn't do. It leads you into everything; you can't leave anything alone. No, no—make sure your tenants don't sell their straw and that sort of thing, and give them drainage tiles, you know. But this fancy farming won't do. It's the dearest whistle you can buy; you might just as well keep a pack of hounds.”

“Surely,” said Dorothea, “it's better to spend money discovering how people can make the best use of the land that supports them all than on keeping dogs and horses merely to gallop across it. There is no sin in making yourself poor through experiments that benefit everyone.”

She spoke more forcefully than was expected of so young a lady, but Sir James had asked her. He often did, and she had often imagined encouraging him in many good deeds once he became her brother-in-law.
While Dorothea spoke, Mr. Casaubon turned his eyes pointedly towards her and seemed to notice her afresh.

“Young ladies don't understand political economy, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, smiling at Mr. Casaubon. “I remember when we all read Adam Smith. Now _there's_ a book. At one time I absorbed every new idea—human perfectibility, for instance. But some say history goes round in circles, and you can make a very good case for that; I've argued it myself. The truth is that human reason can take you a little too far—over the hedge, in fact. It took me quite a distance once, but I saw it wouldn't do. I reined in, reined in just in time. Not too sharply, though. I've always favoured a little theory. We must have Thought, or we'll find ourselves back in the dark ages. But speaking of books, there's Southey's ‘Peninsular War.’ I'm reading it in the mornings. Do you know Southey?”

“No,” said Mr. Casaubon, unable to keep up with Mr. Brooke's headlong reasoning and thinking only of the book. “At present I have little time for literature of that sort. Lately I have been wearing out my eyes over ancient scripts. In fact, I need someone to read to me in the evenings. But I am particular about voices and cannot bear listening to an inadequate reader. In some ways it is unfortunate: I draw too much nourishment from inward sources; I spend too much time among the dead. My mind is rather like an ancient man's ghost, wandering the world and trying to reconstruct it in thought as it once was, despite its ruins and bewildering changes. Still, I find I must take the greatest care of my eyesight.”

This was Mr. Casaubon's first extended speech. He spoke precisely, as if required to make a public statement. The neat, balanced rise and fall of his delivery, occasionally accompanied by a nod, stood out all the more against good Mr. Brooke's slovenly fragments. Dorothea told herself he was the most interesting man she had ever met, not even excepting Monsieur Liret, the Vaudois clergyman who had lectured on Waldensian history. To reconstruct a vanished world, surely in the service of truth's highest purposes—what work to witness in any capacity, to help with even by holding a lamp! That uplifting thought carried her above her annoyance at being teased about her ignorance of political economy, that science which was never explained and was brought down like a snuffer on every light she kindled.

“But you enjoy riding, Miss Brooke,” Sir James managed to say presently. “I would have thought you could appreciate some of the pleasures of hunting. I wish you'd let me send a chestnut horse over for you to try. He's been trained for a lady. On Saturday I saw you cantering over the hill on a horse quite unworthy of you. My groom can bring Corydon every day; you need only name the hour.”

“Thank you, you're very kind. I intend to give up riding. I won't ride again,” Dorothea said. She was driven to this abrupt decision by irritation that Sir James kept claiming her attention when she wanted to give it all to Mr. Casaubon.
“No, that's too harsh,” Sir James said, his reproachful tone revealing his keen concern. “Your sister is inclined to self-denial, isn't she?” he went on, turning to Celia on his right.
“I think she is,” Celia replied, afraid of saying something her sister would dislike and blushing as prettily as possible above her necklace. “She enjoys giving things up.”
“If that were true, Celia, giving things up would be self-indulgence for me, not self-denial. But there can be good reasons for choosing not to do something very pleasant,” Dorothea said.
Mr. Brooke was talking at the same moment, but Mr. Casaubon was clearly watching Dorothea, and she knew it.
“Exactly,” Sir James said. “You give things up for some noble, generous reason.”

“No, really, not exactly. I didn't say that about myself,” Dorothea replied, turning red. Unlike Celia she seldom blushed, and only from intense delight or anger. Just now it was anger at the contrary Sir James. Why couldn't he attend to Celia and let her listen to Mr. Casaubon? If only that learned man would talk instead of letting Mr. Brooke talk at him. Her uncle was explaining that the Reformation either meant something or it didn't; that he himself was Protestant to the core, but Catholicism was a fact; and as for refusing an acre of one's land for a Romanist chapel, all men needed religion's bridle, which, properly understood, meant fear of the Hereafter.

“I made quite a study of theology once,” Mr. Brooke said, as though accounting for the insight he had just displayed. “I know a little of every school. I knew Wilberforce in his best days. Do you know Wilberforce?”
Mr. Casaubon's answer was “No.”
“Well, perhaps Wilberforce wasn't enough of a thinker. But if I entered Parliament, as people have asked me to do, I'd sit as an independent, as Wilberforce did, and work for philanthropic causes.”
Mr. Casaubon inclined his head and remarked that the field was broad.

“Yes,” Mr. Brooke replied with an easy smile, “but I have documents. I started collecting them a long time ago. They need putting in order, but whenever a question caught my attention I've written to someone and received an answer. I have documents to support me. Now, how do you organize yours?”
“Partly in pigeonholes,” Mr. Casaubon replied, looking rather startled by the effort required.
“Ah, pigeonholes won't do. I've tried those, but everything gets muddled in them. I never know whether a paper is under A or Z.”
“I wish you'd let me organize your papers, uncle,” Dorothea said. “I'd give them all letters and then list the subjects under each one.”
Mr. Casaubon smiled in solemn approval and said to Mr. Brooke, “You see, you have an excellent secretary ready to hand.”
“No, no,” said Mr. Brooke with a shake of his head. “I can't have young ladies interfering with my documents. They're too flighty.”

Dorothea was hurt. Mr. Casaubon would suppose her uncle had some particular reason for saying this. In reality, the remark rested in his mind as lightly as a broken insect's wing among all its other scraps, and a passing current had blown it onto _her_.
Once the girls were alone together in the drawing room, Celia said—
“How dreadfully ugly Mr. Casaubon is!”
“Celia! He's one of the most distinguished-looking men I've ever seen. He looks remarkably like Locke's portrait. His eyes have those same deep sockets.”
“Did Locke have those two white moles with hairs growing out of them?”
“Oh, very likely! When a certain sort of person looked at him,” Dorothea replied, walking a little way off.
“Mr. Casaubon has such a yellow complexion.”
“So much the better. I suppose you prefer a man with skin like a _cochon de lait_.”
“Dodo!” Celia exclaimed, watching her in surprise. “I've never heard you compare anyone to that before.”
“Why would I have said it before I had a reason? It's a good comparison. The likeness is exact.”
Miss Brooke was plainly forgetting her manners, and Celia thought so too.
“I'm surprised at you losing your temper, Dorothea.”
“It's so painful, Celia, that you insist on seeing human beings as nothing more than dressed-up animals, and never recognize a great soul in a man's face.”
“Does Mr. Casaubon have a great soul?” There was a little innocent malice in Celia's question.
“Yes, I believe he does,” Dorothea answered in a firm, full voice. “Everything I observe in him agrees with his pamphlet on Biblical Cosmology.”
“He doesn't say very much,” Celia remarked.
“He has nobody here he can talk to.”

Celia thought privately, “Dorothea quite despises Sir James Chettam. I don't believe she'd accept him.” She felt that was a pity. She had never mistaken the object of the baronet's interest. Sometimes she had reflected that Dodo might not make a husband happy if he did not share her outlook. Buried deep in her heart was the feeling that her sister was too religious for a comfortable family life. Her principles and scruples were like spilled needles, making one afraid to walk, to sit, or even to eat.

When Miss Brooke sat at the tea table, Sir James came to sit beside her, having found nothing offensive in her earlier answers. Why would he? He thought she probably liked him, and behaviour must be very emphatic before people stop interpreting it through their own confident or suspicious expectations. She charmed him completely, though naturally he had formed a little theory about his attachment. He was made of excellent human dough and had the rare virtue of knowing that his abilities, even unleashed, would not set the smallest stream in the county on fire. So he liked the prospect of a wife he could ask, “What shall we do?” about one thing or another; someone who could supply her husband with reasons, and whose property would also qualify her to do so. As for Miss Brooke's alleged excess of religion, his idea of what it amounted to was very vague, and he expected marriage to extinguish it. In short, he felt he had fallen in love in the right quarter and was prepared to accept a great deal of female ascendancy, which a man, after all, could always suppress whenever he chose. Sir James could not imagine ever wishing to suppress this handsome girl's ascendancy; her cleverness delighted him. Why shouldn't it? A man's mind—whatever there is of it—always has the advantage of being male, just as the smallest birch belongs to a higher order than the loftiest palm. Even his ignorance is of a sounder kind. Sir James may not have invented this judgment, but a kindly Providence provides even the limpest personality with a little stiffening glue or starch in the shape of tradition.
“I hope you'll reconsider your decision about the horse, Miss Brooke,” her persistent admirer said. “I assure you, there's no healthier exercise than riding.”
“I know that,” Dorothea answered coldly. “I think it would benefit Celia—if she would take it up.”
“But you're such an accomplished rider yourself.”
“Forgive me, but I've had very little practice, and a horse could throw me easily.”
“Then you have all the more reason to practise. Every lady should be an accomplished rider so that she can ride with her husband.”

“You see how far apart our views are, Sir James. I've decided I ought not to become an accomplished rider, so I'd never fit your ideal of a lady.” Dorothea stared straight ahead and spoke with chilly abruptness, looking very much like a handsome boy. The contrast with her admirer's anxious good nature was amusing.
“I'd like to know what reasons you have for such a cruel decision. Surely you can't think riding is wrong.”
“It's perfectly possible for me to think it would be wrong for me.”
“But why?” Sir James protested in a gentle, tender voice.
Mr. Casaubon had approached the table with his teacup and stood listening.

“We should not probe motives too closely,” he interjected in his measured manner. “Miss Brooke knows they tend to weaken when expressed: their fragrance mingles with the coarser air. We must keep the sprouting seed out of the light.”

Dorothea flushed with pleasure and looked up at him gratefully. Here was a man who understood the higher inward life, with whom spiritual communion was possible; more than that, who could illuminate moral principle with the broadest knowledge. His learning almost proved the truth of whatever he believed!

Dorothea's conclusions may seem sweeping, but life could hardly have continued in any age without this generous allowance of inferences, which makes marriage possible amid civilization's difficulties. Has anyone ever squeezed the cobweb of premarital acquaintance down to the tiny pill it really amounts to?
“Certainly,” the good Sir James agreed. “We mustn't press Miss Brooke for reasons she'd prefer not to discuss. I'm sure they would do her credit.”

He felt no jealousy at the interest in Dorothea's upward glance towards Mr. Casaubon. It never entered his head that a girl he was considering marrying could care for a dried-up bookworm approaching fifty, except in a religious sort of way, as she might for a clergyman of some standing.

Still, since Miss Brooke had begun talking to Mr. Casaubon about the Vaudois clergy, Sir James went over to Celia and spoke to her about her sister. He mentioned a house in town and asked whether Miss Brooke disliked London. Away from Dorothea, Celia talked freely, and Sir James reflected that the younger Miss Brooke was certainly very agreeable as well as pretty, though not, as some claimed, cleverer or more sensible than her older sister. He felt he had chosen the one who was superior in every respect. Naturally a man likes to expect the best. A bachelor who pretended not to would be a very Mawworm of hypocrisy.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter III
paragraphs:
“Tell, goddess, what followed when Raphael,
The kindly archangel . . .
Eve
Listened closely to the story, filled
With wonder and deep thought as she heard
Of things so lofty and so strange.”
—_Paradise Lost_, Book vii.

If Mr. Casaubon really had begun to consider Miss Brooke a suitable wife, the reasons that could persuade her to accept him were already planted in her mind. By the following evening they had budded and blossomed. That morning they had talked at length, while Celia, who did not enjoy the company of Mr. Casaubon's moles and yellow complexion, escaped to the vicarage to play with the curate's cheerful, poorly shod children.

By now Dorothea had gazed deep into the unmeasured reservoir of Mr. Casaubon's mind. There she saw every quality she herself possessed reflected back in vague, labyrinthine expanses. She had shared much of her own experience with him and learned the scope of his great work, which also stretched into an enticing labyrinth. He had instructed her like Milton's “affable archangel,” and with something of that angel's manner explained his undertaking. He would show that every system of myth, every stray fragment of myth in the world, was a corrupted form of an originally revealed tradition. Others had attempted this before, admittedly, but without the thoroughness, fairness of comparison and effective arrangement he intended. Once one had grasped the true position and stood firmly upon it, the vast field of mythological structures became intelligible—indeed, shone with the reflected light of their correspondences. Gathering that great harvest of truth, however, was neither quick nor easy. His notes already filled a formidable row of volumes. The crowning labour would be to compress these abundant and still accumulating findings so that, like the earlier harvest of Hippocratic books, they fitted on one small shelf. Mr. Casaubon explained all this to Dorothea much as he would to a fellow scholar: he did not command two different styles of conversation. True, whenever he used Greek or Latin he scrupulously supplied the English, but he would probably have done that in any company. A learned country clergyman habitually thinks of his acquaintances as “lords, knights, and other noble and worthy men, who know but little Latin.”

The breadth of this conception utterly captivated Dorothea. Here was something beyond the shallows of schoolroom literature for young ladies. Here was a living Bossuet, whose work would bring complete knowledge into harmony with devoted faith; a modern Augustine, combining the glories of learned doctor and saint.

His holiness seemed as evident as his learning. Dorothea felt moved to speak openly about subjects she could discuss with nobody she had previously met at Tipton. In particular, she spoke of how church forms and statements of belief mattered less than spiritual religion: the surrender of self in communion with Divine perfection which she found expressed in the finest Christian books of widely separated ages. Mr. Casaubon understood her immediately. He assured her that he shared this view, when properly moderated by wise conformity, and could cite historical examples she had never heard of.

“He thinks as I do,” Dorothea told herself, “or rather, his thought contains a whole world of which mine is only a cheap little mirror. And his feelings, his entire experience—what a lake beside my tiny pool!”

Miss Brooke drew conclusions from words and inclinations as readily as any girl her age. Signs are small and measurable; interpretations have no limit. In sweet, passionate girls, any sign may summon wonder, hope and belief as vast as the sky, coloured by the diffusion of a thimbleful of knowledge. They are not always very badly deceived. Even Sinbad may by chance have given a true account, and faulty reasoning sometimes brings poor mortals to correct conclusions. Starting far from the right point, then travelling in loops and zigzags, we occasionally reach exactly where we ought to be. Miss Brooke's haste in trusting therefore does not prove Mr. Casaubon unworthy of her trust.

He stayed a little longer than planned, yielding to mild pressure from Mr. Brooke, whose only inducement was his own collection of documents about machine-breaking and hayrick-burning. Summoned to the library, Mr. Casaubon faced a heap of them while his host picked up first one and then another to read aloud. His reading wandered and faltered, jumping from one unfinished passage to the next with a “Yes, now, but here!” Finally he pushed the whole pile aside and opened the diary of his youthful travels on the Continent.

“Look here—this is all about Greece. Rhamnus, the ruins of Rhamnus—you're a great Greek scholar, now. I don't know whether you've studied the topography much. I spent no end of time working these things out—Helicon, for instance. Here, now! ‘Next morning we set out for Parnassus, the twin-peaked Parnassus.’ This whole volume is about Greece, you know,” Mr. Brooke concluded, running his thumb across the edges of the pages as he held the book out.

Mr. Casaubon formed a dignified, if rather sorrowful, audience. He bowed at the right moments and, so far as he could without appearing impatient or dismissive, avoided examining any documents. He remembered that this haphazardness was connected with the country's institutions, and that the man driving him through this punishing mental scramble was not merely a kindly host but a landowner and custos rotulorum, keeper of the county records. Did the thought that Mr. Brooke was Dorothea's uncle also help him endure it?

He certainly seemed increasingly intent on getting her to talk to him, on drawing her out, as Celia privately observed. When he looked at her, a smile often lit his face like pale winter sunshine. Before leaving the next morning, during a pleasant walk with Miss Brooke along the gravel terrace, he mentioned the drawbacks of his solitary life. He felt the need for that cheerful companionship through which youth's presence can lighten or vary the serious labours of maturity. He delivered this statement as precisely and carefully as a diplomatic envoy whose words were expected to have consequences. Indeed, Mr. Casaubon did not generally expect to repeat or revise anything he said about practical or personal matters. An inclination deliberately stated on the second of October should, he thought, need only a reference to that date. He judged by his own memory, a volume in which a vide supra—a “see above”—could replace repetition, rather than the ordinary, much-used blotting book bearing only traces of forgotten writing. In this instance, however, his confidence was unlikely to prove misplaced. Dorothea heard and remembered his words with the eager interest of a fresh young nature for which every new kind of experience marks an epoch.

It was three o'clock on that beautiful, breezy autumn day when Mr. Casaubon drove away to his rectory at Lowick, just five miles from Tipton. Already wearing her bonnet and shawl, Dorothea hurried through the shrubbery and across the park to wander in the wood along its boundary. Her only visible companion was Monk, the great St. Bernard who always guarded the young ladies on their walks. A girl's vision of a possible future had opened before her. She looked towards it with trembling hope and wanted to roam through it uninterrupted. She walked briskly in the brisk air, colour rising in her cheeks, and her straw bonnet slipped slightly backwards—a bonnet our contemporaries might examine with puzzled curiosity, like an obsolete kind of basket. Her portrait would perhaps be incomplete without mentioning that she wore her brown hair in flat braids coiled behind her head, daringly exposing its shape at a time when public taste demanded that nature's scantiness be disguised with high barricades of frizzed curls and bows, surpassed by no great people except the Fijians. This was one sign of Miss Brooke's asceticism. Yet nothing ascetic showed in her bright, full eyes as she looked ahead, not consciously observing but drawing into her intense mood the afternoon's solemn splendour: its long swathes of light between distant rows of lime trees whose shadows met.

Anyone, young or old—anyone, that is, in those days before Reform—would have found her an appealing sight if they had attributed the glow in her eyes and cheeks to the ordinary images of newly awakened young love. Poetry has given ample consecration to Chloe's illusions about Strephon, as it should to the touching beauty of all spontaneous trust. Miss Pippin adoring young Pumpkin, dreaming down endless avenues of tireless companionship, was a little drama our fathers and mothers never tired of, and it had been dressed in every costume. Let Pumpkin merely possess a figure that could survive the disadvantages of a short-waisted tailcoat, and everyone thought it not only natural but necessary to perfect womanhood that a sweet girl should instantly believe in his virtue, his exceptional abilities and, above all, his absolute sincerity. Yet perhaps nobody then alive—certainly nobody near Tipton—could have sympathized with a girl whose dreams of marriage took their colour entirely from an exalted enthusiasm for life's purposes. That enthusiasm burned chiefly on its own fuel and took no account of the details of bridal clothing, the pattern of silverware, or even the honours and tender pleasures of a flourishing married woman.

Dorothea had now begun to think Mr. Casaubon might want her for his wife, and the possibility filled her with a kind of reverent gratitude. How good of him—indeed, it would be almost like a winged messenger suddenly appearing beside her path and extending his hand! For a long time uncertainty had oppressed her, hanging like thick summer haze over her desire to make her life greatly useful. What could she do, what should she do? She was barely more than a girl, yet had an active conscience and a great intellectual hunger that could not be fed by the education offered to girls, with its nibbles and judgments like those of a wandering mouse. Had she possessed a little more stupidity and conceit, she might have thought a wealthy Christian young lady's ideal life lay in village charities, patronizing the poorer clergy, and reading “Female Scripture Characters,” with its revelations of Sara's private experience under the Old Dispensation and Dorcas's under the New. She might have tended her soul over her embroidery in her own sitting room, with marriage in the background to a man less strict than herself—men being involved in affairs religion could not explain—whom she could pray for and advise at suitable moments. Poor Dorothea was excluded from such contentment. The intensity of her religious nature and the power it exerted over her life were only one aspect of a temperament wholly passionate, theoretical and intellectually consistent. Such a nature, struggling in the bonds of a narrow education and enclosed by a social life that seemed merely a maze of petty pursuits, a walled labyrinth of small paths leading nowhere, was bound to appear both excessive and inconsistent to others. Whatever seemed best to her, she wanted to justify with the fullest knowledge, rather than live in a pretended acceptance of rules nobody followed. All her youthful passion still poured into this hunger of the soul. The union that attracted her would release her from a girl's subjection to her own ignorance, giving her the freedom of willingly submitting to a guide who would lead her along the grandest road.

“Then I would learn everything,” she told herself, still walking quickly along the woodland bridleway. “It would be my duty to study, so I could help him better in his great work. Nothing in our lives would be trivial. Our everyday things would stand for the greatest things. It would be like marrying Pascal. I'd learn to recognize truth by the same light that great men have seen it by. Then, when I was older, I'd know what to do. I'd understand how to lead a great life here, now, in England. At present I can't feel certain of doing good in any way. Everything is like going on a mission to people whose language I don't speak—except building decent cottages. There can be no doubt about that. Oh, I hope I could get the people at Lowick properly housed! I'll draw plenty of plans while I have the time.”

Dorothea stopped her thoughts abruptly, reproaching herself for so presumptuously counting on uncertain events. But the appearance of a rider cantering round a bend spared her any inward effort to change their course. The well-groomed chestnut and two handsome setters left no doubt that it was Sir James Chettam. Seeing Dorothea, he dismounted at once, handed his horse to his groom and approached her carrying something white on his arm, at which the two setters barked excitedly.
“How delightful to meet you, Miss Brooke,” he said, lifting his hat to reveal smoothly waved fair hair. “It brings forward a pleasure I'd been looking forward to.”

Miss Brooke resented the interruption. This pleasant baronet, who really would make Celia a suitable husband, overestimated the need to please the older sister. Even a future brother-in-law can become oppressive if he constantly assumes too close an understanding and agrees with you even when you contradict him. The thought that he might mistakenly be courting her could not form: all her mental energy was occupied with convictions of another kind. At this moment he was positively intrusive, and his dimpled hands were quite disagreeable. Irritation made her flush deeply as she returned his greeting with some hauteur.
Sir James read her heightened colour in the way most flattering to himself, and thought he had never seen Miss Brooke look so lovely.

“I've brought a little petitioner,” he said, “or rather, I've brought him to see whether you approve before he makes his petition.” He displayed the white thing under his arm: a tiny Maltese puppy, one of nature's most artless toys.
“It hurts me to see creatures bred solely to be pets,” Dorothea said. Her opinion was forming at that very instant, as opinions do, in the heat of irritation.
“Oh, why is that?” Sir James asked as they walked on.

“I don't believe all the fondling makes them happy. They're too helpless, their lives too fragile. A weasel or mouse that finds its own living is more interesting. I like to imagine the animals around us have souls something like ours, and either conduct their own little business or can be our companions, like Monk here. Those creatures are parasites.”
“I'm so glad to learn you don't like them,” said the good Sir James. “I'd never keep one for myself, but ladies are usually fond of these Maltese dogs. Here, John, would you take this dog?”

Thus the objectionable puppy, with equally black and expressive nose and eyes, was disposed of, since Miss Brooke had decided it would have been better unborn. Still, she felt an explanation was needed.

“You mustn't assume Celia feels as I do. I think she likes little pets. She once had a tiny terrier she loved dearly. It made me anxious because I was afraid I'd step on it. I'm rather short-sighted.”
“You have an opinion of your own about everything, Miss Brooke, and it's invariably a good one.”
What could anyone say in reply to such foolish flattery?
“You know, I envy you that,” Sir James continued as they walked at the fairly brisk pace Dorothea had set.
“I'm not quite sure I understand your meaning.”
“Your ability to reach an opinion. I can judge people; I know when I like someone. But with other things, you know, I often find it hard to decide. You hear very sensible arguments on both sides.”
“Or arguments that sound sensible. Perhaps we don't always distinguish sense from nonsense.”
Dorothea felt she was being rather discourteous.
“Exactly,” said Sir James. “But you seem able to make that distinction.”
“Quite the opposite: I often can't decide. But that's because I don't know enough. The right answer still exists, even if I can't see it.”

“I think few people would see it sooner. You know, Lovegood told me yesterday you had the best idea imaginable for a cottage plan—quite extraordinary in a young lady, he thought. You had real _genus_, as he put it. He said you wanted Mr. Brooke to build a new group of cottages, though he seemed to doubt your uncle would agree. Now, that's something I want to do myself—on my own estate, I mean. I'd be delighted to put your plan into practice, if you'd let me see it. Of course, you don't get your money back; that's why people object. Labourers can never pay enough rent to make it profitable. Even so, it's worth doing.”

“Worth doing! Yes, indeed,” Dorothea said passionately, forgetting her earlier petty irritations. “We deserve to be driven out of our lovely houses with a whip of small cords—all of us who let our tenants live in the pigsties we see around us. Life in a cottage could be happier than ours, if the cottages were proper homes fit for human beings from whom we expect duty and affection.”
“Would you let me look at your plan?”

“Yes, certainly. I'm sure it has plenty of faults. But I've studied all the cottage plans in Loudon's book and selected what seemed best in them. Oh, how happy I'd be to set an example round here! I think instead of Lazarus at the gate, we should put those pigsty cottages outside the park gates.”

Dorothea was now in the happiest mood. Sir James as her brother-in-law, building model cottages on his estate; perhaps others built at Lowick, then more and more elsewhere in imitation—it would be as though Oberlin's spirit had swept through the parishes and made poverty's life beautiful!

Sir James examined all the plans and took one away to discuss with Lovegood. He also carried away a satisfied feeling that he was advancing rapidly in Miss Brooke's esteem. The Maltese puppy was never offered to Celia. Dorothea later remembered this omission with surprise, but blamed herself: she had monopolized Sir James. Still, it was a relief to have no puppy underfoot.

Celia was there while the plans were studied, and noticed Sir James's delusion. “He thinks Dodo cares for him, when she only cares for her plans. Yet I'm not sure she'd refuse him if she thought he'd let her direct everything and carry out all her ideas. And how uncomfortable Sir James would be! I can't bear ideas.”

Indulging this dislike was Celia's private luxury. She dared not state it outright to her sister, since that would invite a demonstration that she was somehow opposed to goodness itself. On safe occasions, however, she found indirect ways to bring her negative wisdom to bear on Dorothea. She could pull her sister out of rapture by reminding her that people were staring rather than listening. Celia was not impulsive. Whatever she wanted to say could wait, and it always emerged in the same quiet, evenly clipped manner. When others spoke with energy and emphasis, she merely watched their faces and features. She could never understand how well-bred people agreed to sing, opening their mouths in the absurd way that exercise required.

Within a few days Mr. Casaubon called one morning and was invited to dine and stay overnight the following week. Dorothea thus had three more conversations with him and became convinced her first impressions were correct. He was everything she had imagined. Almost every remark seemed a specimen brought up from a mine, or an inscription over a museum door that might open onto the treasures of past ages. Her faith in his intellectual riches grew deeper and worked more powerfully upon her affections because it was now clear he came to see her. This accomplished man stooped to notice a young girl and took the trouble to address her understanding, rather than offer foolish compliments, sometimes even correcting her instructively. What delightful companionship! Mr. Casaubon seemed unaware that trivial matters existed. He never passed round the small talk of ponderous men, as welcome as stale wedding cake smelling of the cupboard. He spoke about what interested him or kept silent, bowing with melancholy courtesy. Dorothea found this adorably genuine: a religious refusal of the artificiality that exhausts the soul in pretence. She revered his spiritual superiority to her as much as his intellect and scholarship. He agreed with her expressions of devotion, usually supplying a fitting quotation. He permitted himself to mention spiritual struggles in his youth. In short, Dorothea believed she could count on understanding, sympathy and guidance here. On one subject—just one—dear to her, she was disappointed. Mr. Casaubon apparently took no interest in building cottages. He turned the conversation towards the extremely cramped homes of the ancient Egyptians, as if to discourage excessively high standards. After he left, his indifference troubled her. Her mind busied itself with arguments about differences of climate that change human needs, and the acknowledged wickedness of pagan despots. Shouldn't she put these arguments to him next time? Further reflection, however, told her she was presumptuous to claim his attention for such a topic. He would not object to her pursuing it in spare moments, as other women expected to occupy themselves with clothes and embroidery; he would not forbid it when—Dorothea felt rather ashamed to catch herself speculating like this. But her uncle had been invited to spend a couple of days at Lowick. Was it reasonable to suppose Mr. Casaubon enjoyed Mr. Brooke's company for its own sake, with or without documents?

Meanwhile that small disappointment increased her pleasure in Sir James Chettam's eagerness to begin the improvements she wanted. He visited much more often than Mr. Casaubon, and she stopped finding him disagreeable once he proved so thoroughly serious. He had already applied considerable practical ability to Lovegood's estimates, and was charmingly willing to follow her lead. She suggested building two cottages and moving two families out of their old hovels, which could then be demolished and replaced on the same sites. Sir James said “Exactly,” and she tolerated the word remarkably well.

Certainly men with so few ideas of their own could be very useful members of society under sound feminine guidance—provided they chose their sisters-in-law well! It is hard to say whether she was being a little wilful in remaining blind to the possibility that a different kind of choice concerning her was at stake. Just now, however, her life overflowed with hope and activity. Besides considering her plans, she took learned books from the library and hurried through many subjects so that she might be a little less ignorant in conversation with Mr. Casaubon. All the while her conscience kept asking whether she was overvaluing these poor efforts and viewing them with that self-satisfaction which is the final doom of ignorance and folly.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter IV
paragraphs: 1st Gentleman. Our actions are the chains we forge for ourselves.
2nd Gentleman. Yes, that's true; but I think the world supplies the iron.
“Sir James seems determined to do whatever you want,” Celia said as they drove home after inspecting the new building site.
“He's a good soul, and more sensible than anyone would expect,” Dorothea answered without thinking.
“You mean he seems rather foolish.”
“No, no,” Dorothea said, checking herself and briefly resting her hand on her sister's. “But he doesn't speak equally well about every subject.”
“I should think only disagreeable people do that,” Celia replied in her usual purring tone. “They must be dreadful to live with. Just imagine! At breakfast, and all the time.”

Dorothea laughed. “Oh, Kitty, what a wonderful creature you are!” She pinched Celia's chin, now inclined to find her irresistibly lovely and charming, fitted to become an everlasting cherub, and, if doctrine allowed one to say it, scarcely more in need of salvation than a squirrel. “Of course people needn't always talk well. It's only that you can judge the quality of their minds when they try to.”
“You mean Sir James makes the attempt and fails.”
“I was making a general remark. Why are you interrogating me about Sir James? Pleasing me isn't the purpose of his life.”
“Really, Dodo, can you honestly believe that?”

“Certainly. He sees me as a future sister, nothing more.” Dorothea had never hinted at this before. A shyness about such matters, shared by both sisters, had made her wait for some decisive event to introduce it. Celia blushed, but immediately replied—

“Please stop making that mistake, Dodo. When Tantripp brushed my hair the other day, she told me Sir James's servant had heard from Mrs. Cadwallader's maid that Sir James was going to marry the older Miss Brooke.”

“How can you let Tantripp gossip like that to you, Celia?” Dorothea said indignantly. She was no less angry because details asleep in her memory were waking up to confirm this unwelcome discovery. “You must have questioned her. It's degrading.”

“I see no harm whatever in Tantripp talking to me. It's better to hear what people are saying. You see the mistakes you make by getting ideas into your head. I'm perfectly sure Sir James intends to propose, and he thinks you'll accept him, especially since you've been so pleased with him over the plans. And uncle too—I know he expects it. Anyone can see Sir James is very much in love with you.”

The reversal in Dorothea's mind was so violent and painful that tears welled up and poured down. Every cherished plan turned bitter. She was disgusted to imagine Sir James believing she acknowledged him as her lover. She was distressed on Celia's account as well.
“How could he expect that?” she burst out with her greatest vehemence. “I've never agreed with him about anything except the cottages. Before that I was scarcely even polite.”
“But you've been so pleased with him ever since. He's begun to feel quite certain you're fond of him.”
“Fond of him, Celia! How can you use such a hateful expression?” Dorothea demanded passionately.
“Goodness, Dorothea, I imagine being fond of a man would be proper enough if you accepted him as your husband.”
“It offends me to hear that Sir James could suppose I was fond of him. Besides, that isn't the right word for what I would need to feel towards a man I agreed to marry.”

“Well, I'm sorry for Sir James. I thought I ought to tell you, because you were carrying on as usual, never looking where you are and stepping in the wrong place. You always see things nobody else sees, and it's impossible to satisfy you; yet you never notice what's perfectly plain. That's your way, Dodo.” Something had certainly lent Celia unusual courage. She was not sparing the sister she sometimes held in awe. Who knows what fair criticisms Murr the Cat may be making of us creatures with our wider speculations?

“It's very painful,” Dorothea said, feeling whipped. “I can't have anything more to do with the cottages. I must be rude to him. I must tell him I want no part in them. It's very painful.” Tears filled her eyes again.

“Wait a little and think it over. You know he's going away for a day or two to visit his sister. There'll only be Lovegood.” Celia could not help softening. “Poor Dodo,” she continued in kindly clipped phrases. “It is hard. Drawing plans is your favourite _fad_.”

“A _fad_ for drawing plans! Do you think I care about my fellow creatures' homes in that childish way? No wonder I make mistakes. How can anyone ever do anything nobly Christian among people whose thoughts are so petty?”

They said no more. Dorothea was too shaken to recover her composure and behave in a way that admitted any fault of her own. She preferred to blame the intolerable narrowness and half-blind conscience of the society around her. Celia was no longer an eternal cherub but a thorn in her spirit, a pink-and-white unbeliever, worse than any discouraging figure in “Pilgrim's Progress.” The _fad_ for drawing plans! What was life worth, what great faith could exist, if the entire meaning of one's actions could shrivel into such dried-up rubbish? When she stepped out of the carriage her cheeks were pale and her eyelids red. She looked the picture of sorrow. Her uncle, meeting her in the hall, would have been alarmed if Celia had not stood beside her looking so pretty and calm that he immediately attributed Dorothea's tears to excessive religion. During their absence he had returned from the county town, where he had gone concerning a petition to pardon a criminal.
“Well, my dears,” he said kindly as they came to kiss him, “I hope nothing unpleasant has happened while I've been away.”
“No, uncle,” Celia answered. “We've been to Freshitt to see the cottages. We expected you home for lunch.”
“I stopped at Lowick for lunch—you didn't know I'd come through Lowick. And I've brought two pamphlets for you, Dorothea. In the library, you know; they're on the library table.”

An electric current seemed to pass through Dorothea, thrilling her out of despair into expectation. The pamphlets concerned the early Church. She shook off the oppression of Celia, Tantripp and Sir James and went straight to the library. Celia went upstairs. A message detained Mr. Brooke, but when he returned to the library he found Dorothea seated, already absorbed in a pamphlet with some notes by Mr. Casaubon in the margins. She took it in as eagerly as she might have breathed the fragrance of fresh flowers after a dry, hot, dreary walk.
She was escaping Tipton and Freshitt, and her own unhappy tendency to put her feet wrong on the road to the New Jerusalem.

Mr. Brooke settled in his armchair and stretched his legs towards the wood fire, now collapsed into a marvellous mass of glowing dice between the firedogs. Gently rubbing his hands, he looked mildly at Dorothea with an unhurried, neutral air, as though he had nothing particular to say. As soon as she noticed him, she closed her pamphlet and stood as if to leave. Usually she would have taken an interest in his errand of mercy for the criminal, but her recent distress had left her distracted.

“I came back by Lowick, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, apparently not to stop her leaving but from his usual inclination to repeat himself. This fundamental principle of human speech showed especially clearly in Mr. Brooke. “I lunched there and saw Casaubon's library and that sort of thing. The air's sharp when you're driving. Won't you sit down, my dear? You look cold.”

Dorothea was quite willing to accept. When her uncle's easy way of taking things did not happen to exasperate her, it could be soothing. She took off her bonnet and cloak and sat opposite him, enjoying the heat while raising her beautiful hands to shield her face. They were neither thin nor small, but strong, feminine, motherly hands. She seemed to hold them up in atonement for her passionate desire to know and think, which in the unfriendly atmosphere of Tipton and Freshitt had ended in tears and reddened eyelids.
Now she remembered the condemned prisoner. “What news have you brought about the sheep thief, uncle?”
“What, poor Bunch? Well, it seems we can't save him. He's to be hanged.”
Dorothea's brow registered both condemnation and pity.
“Hanged, you know,” Mr. Brooke repeated with a quiet nod. “Poor Romilly! He'd have helped us. I knew Romilly. Casaubon didn't. He's rather buried in his books, you know, Casaubon is.”
“When a man has great studies to pursue and a great work to write, of course he has to give up much social life. How can he go round making acquaintances?”

“True enough. But a man gets gloomy, you know. I've always been a bachelor myself, but my temperament kept me from moping. I used to go everywhere and take everything in. I never moped. But I can see Casaubon does, you know. He needs a companion—a companion, you know.”
“Being his companion would be a great honour for anyone,” Dorothea said with energy.

“You like him, do you?” Mr. Brooke said without surprise or any other visible emotion. “Well, I've known Casaubon ten years, ever since he came to Lowick. But I've never got anything out of him—ideas, you know. Still, he's a first-rate man and might become a bishop, that sort of thing, if Peel stays in office. And he thinks very highly of you, my dear.”
Dorothea found herself unable to speak.

“The fact is, his opinion of you is very high indeed. And he expresses himself remarkably well, Casaubon does. He's deferred to me because you haven't come of age. In short, I promised to speak to you, though I told him I thought his chances were small. I had to tell him that. My niece is very young, I said, and that kind of thing. But I didn't think I needed to go into everything. Anyway, the long and short of it is that he has asked my permission to propose marriage to you—marriage, you know,” Mr. Brooke said with his explanatory nod. “I thought I'd better tell you, my dear.”

Nothing in Mr. Brooke's manner betrayed anxiety, but he genuinely wanted to know his niece's thoughts so he could offer timely advice if needed. Whatever feeling he could find room for, as a magistrate who had absorbed so many ideas, was entirely kind. When Dorothea did not answer at once, he repeated, “I thought I'd better tell you, my dear.”
“Thank you, uncle,” Dorothea said clearly and steadily. “I'm deeply grateful to Mr. Casaubon. If he proposes, I'll accept him. I admire and respect him more than any man I've ever met.”

After a short pause Mr. Brooke said slowly, in a low voice, “Ah? … Well! In some ways he's a good match. But now, Chettam is a good match too, and our estates adjoin. I'll never oppose your wishes, my dear. People should have their own way in marriage and such things—up to a point, you know. I've always said that: up to a point. I want you to marry well, and I have good reason to think Chettam wants to marry you. I only mention it, you know.”
“I could never possibly marry Sir James Chettam,” Dorothea said. “If he has any thought of marrying me, he's badly mistaken.”
“That's just it, you see. You never can tell. I'd have thought Chettam exactly the sort of man a woman would like.”
“Please don't speak of him in that way again, uncle,” Dorothea said, feeling her earlier irritation return.

Mr. Brooke marvelled. Women, he felt, were an inexhaustible subject of study, since even at his age he could not predict them with scientific accuracy. Here was a fellow like Chettam without the slightest chance.

“Well, but Casaubon, now. There's no rush—not for you, I mean. Every year will make a difference to him, it's true. He's over forty-five, you know. A good twenty-seven years older than you, I'd say. Still, if it's learning and standing you like, and that sort of thing, we can't have everything. His income is good; he has a handsome estate apart from the Church. A good income. But he isn't young, and I mustn't hide from you, my dear, that I don't think his health is especially strong. I know nothing else against him.”
“I wouldn't want a husband very close to my own age,” Dorothea said with solemn conviction. “I'd want one whose judgment and knowledge were superior to mine in every way.”
Mr. Brooke repeated his quiet “Ah? I thought you had more opinions of your own than most girls. I thought you liked your own opinions—liked them, you know.”
“I can't imagine living without opinions, but I'd want sound reasons for them. A wise man could help me understand which opinions rested on the strongest foundations, and help me live by them.”

“Very true. You couldn't put it better—couldn't put it better beforehand, you know. But things turn out oddly,” Mr. Brooke continued, his conscience genuinely urging him to do his best for his niece. “Life isn't poured into a mould, isn't measured out by rule and line and that sort of thing. I never married, and you and yours will benefit from that. The truth is, I never loved anyone enough to put my head into a noose for them. It _is_ a noose, you know. Temper, for instance. There's temper to consider. And a husband likes to be master.”
“I know I must expect difficulties, uncle. Marriage brings higher duties. I've never thought of it simply as personal comfort,” said poor Dorothea.

“Well, you aren't fond of display, a grand household, balls, dinners and all that. I can see Casaubon's habits might suit you better than Chettam's. You shall do as you choose, my dear. I wouldn't obstruct Casaubon; I said that immediately. You never know how anything will turn out. Your tastes aren't the same as every young lady's, and a clergyman and scholar—perhaps a future bishop, that sort of thing—might suit you better than Chettam. Chettam's a good fellow, sound at heart, you know, but he doesn't take much interest in ideas. I did at his age. But Casaubon's eyes, now. I think he's damaged them a little with too much reading.”
“The more opportunity I had to help him, uncle, the happier I would be,” Dorothea said fervently.

“I see you've quite decided. Well, my dear, the truth is that I have a letter for you in my pocket.” Mr. Brooke handed it to her, but as she stood to leave he added, “There's no great hurry, my dear. Think it over, you know.”

After Dorothea left, he reflected that he had certainly spoken forcefully. He had set out the risks of marriage in a striking way, as duty required. But as for claiming to know better than young people—no uncle, however widely he had travelled in youth, however many new ideas he had absorbed or famous people now dead he had dined with, could claim to judge what marriage would suit a girl who preferred Casaubon to Chettam. In short, woman was a problem before which Mr. Brooke's mind went blank, and could therefore scarcely be less complicated than the rotations of an irregular solid.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter V
paragraphs: “Intense scholars commonly suffer from gout, catarrh, discharges, wasting, slow digestion, weak eyes, stones and colic, indigestion, blockages, dizziness, wind, consumption, and all such ailments as come from sitting too much. Most are thin, dried up, unhealthy in colour … all through excessive effort and extraordinary study. If you doubt this, look at the works of the great Tostatus and Thomas Aquinas, and tell me whether those men laboured.”—BURTON'S _Anatomy of Melancholy_, Part I, section 2.
Here is the letter Mr. Casaubon wrote.

MY DEAR MISS BROOKE,—Your guardian has permitted me to write to you on a matter closer to my heart than any other. I trust I am right in seeing more than a coincidence of dates in the fact that I became aware of a need in my own life just when the possibility of knowing you arose. Within the first hour of our meeting, I felt you were eminently, perhaps uniquely, fitted to meet that need. I may say that this need involved stirrings of affection which even my absorption in a work too specialized to abandon could not continually conceal. Every subsequent opportunity to observe you has deepened that impression, convincing me still more strongly of the suitability I first perceived, and so calling forth more decisively the affections I have just mentioned. Our conversations have, I think, sufficiently explained the character of my life and purposes—a character I know is unsuited to the more ordinary kind of mind. In you, however, I have recognized an elevation of thought and a capacity for devotion which I had never supposed could accompany either youth's early bloom or those feminine graces that both win distinction and bestow it when joined, as they notably are in you, to the intellectual qualities already described. I confess I had not hoped to find this rare union of the substantial and the attractive, suited both to assist with serious labours and to lend charm to unoccupied hours. Had I not been introduced to you—an event which, let me repeat, I trust is not merely coincidental with those emerging needs, but providentially connected to them as stages in completing a life's plan—I would presumably have continued to the end without trying to relieve my solitude through marriage. Such, my dear Miss Brooke, is an accurate account of my feelings. Relying on your kindly indulgence, I now venture to ask how far your own feelings might confirm my happy anticipation. I would regard your accepting me as your husband and the earthly guardian of your welfare as the highest gift of Providence. In return I can at least offer an affection not previously spent, and the faithful dedication of a life which, however little of it remains, contains no past pages where, should you turn them, you would discover records that could rightly give you either bitterness or shame. I await your feelings with an anxiety that wisdom would advise me, if possible, to divert through harder work than usual. But in this kind of experience I am still young. When I consider an unfavourable outcome, I cannot help feeling that resignation to solitude will be harder after hope has briefly lit it.

Whatever your answer, I shall remain,
Yours in sincere devotion,
EDWARD CASAUBON.

Dorothea trembled as she read, then dropped to her knees, covered her face and sobbed. She could not pray. In the flood of solemn feeling, thoughts blurred and images drifted uncertainly; she could only cast herself, with a child's sense of resting, into the lap of a divine consciousness that sustained her own. She stayed like that until it was time to dress for dinner.

How could she have thought of examining the letter critically as a declaration of love? The fact that a fuller life was opening before her possessed her whole soul. She was a novice about to enter a higher degree of initiation. Now there would be room for the energies that stirred restlessly beneath the obscurity and weight of her ignorance and the petty tyranny of the world's habits.

Now she could devote herself to duties both great and definite; now she could live constantly in the light of a mind she revered. This hope also glowed with proud delight: a girl's joyful surprise at being chosen by the man her admiration had chosen. All Dorothea's passion passed through a mind striving towards an ideal life. The radiance of her transformed girlhood fell on the first object within its reach. The day's small events, which had stirred her dissatisfaction with her actual circumstances, added force to the speed with which inclination became resolve.

After dinner, while Celia played an “air, with variations”—a little tinkling representative of the artistic part of the girls' education—Dorothea went upstairs to answer Mr. Casaubon. Why delay? She wrote the letter three times, not to alter its words but because her hand was unusually unsteady. She could not bear to have him think her handwriting poor or illegible.
