She prided herself on a hand in which each letter could be identified without extensive guesswork, and intended to make much use of this skill to spare his eyes. Three times she wrote.

MY DEAR MR. CASAUBON,—I am deeply grateful that you love me and consider me worthy to become your wife. I can imagine no greater happiness than one inseparable from yours. To say more would only repeat the same thing at greater length, for I can think of nothing now except the hope that throughout life I may remain

Devotedly yours,
DOROTHEA BROOKE.

Later that evening she followed her uncle into the library and gave him the letter to send in the morning. He was surprised, but showed it only by a few moments of silence. He moved various things about on his desk, then stood with his back to the fire and his glasses on his nose, looking at the address on Dorothea's letter.
“Have you given this enough thought, my dear?” he finally asked.
“I didn't need to think for long, uncle. I know of no reason to hesitate. Anything that changed my mind would have to be important and entirely new to me.”
“Ah! So you've accepted him? Then Chettam has no chance? Has he offended you—offended you, you know? What don't you like about Chettam?”
“There's nothing about him that I do like,” Dorothea answered rather hastily.
Mr. Brooke jerked his head and shoulders back as if somebody had tossed a small object at him. Dorothea immediately reproached herself and added—
“I mean as a husband. I think he's very kind—really very good about the cottages. A man with good intentions.”

“But you must have a scholar and all that? Well, it does run in our family a little. I had it myself—that love of knowledge, looking into everything. A little too much; it carried me too far. It doesn't often run down the female line, though. Or it goes underground like those rivers in Greece, you know, then comes out in the sons. Clever sons, clever mothers. I studied that quite a bit once. Still, my dear, I've always said people should do as they choose in these matters, up to a point. As your guardian I couldn't have agreed to a bad match. But Casaubon has good standing, a good position. I'm afraid Chettam will be hurt, though, and Mrs. Cadwallader will blame me.”

Of course Celia knew nothing of these events that evening. She put Dorothea's distracted manner, and the signs of more tears since they came home, down to her anger about Sir James Chettam and the cottages. She took care not to cause further offence. Once she had said her piece, Celia had no wish to revisit unpleasant subjects. Even as a child she never quarrelled with anyone; she simply observed with surprise that they quarrelled with her and looked like turkey-cocks, then was ready to play cat's cradle as soon as they recovered. Dorothea had always found something wrong in her sister's remarks, though Celia privately protested that she only ever said how things were, nothing more. She never did, and never could, invent things to say out of her own head. But Dodo's great virtue was that she did not stay angry for long. Now, despite their scarcely having spoken all evening, when Celia put her work away to go to bed—as she always did much earlier—Dorothea spoke from the low stool where she had sat, unable to do anything but think. In moments of deep, quiet feeling, her musical voice made her words sound like a beautiful passage of recitative—
“Celia, dear, come here and kiss me,” she said, opening her arms.
Celia knelt to reach the right height and gave her a little butterfly kiss. Dorothea gently wrapped her arms around her and solemnly kissed first one cheek, then the other.
“Don't stay up, Dodo. You're so pale tonight. Go to bed soon,” Celia said comfortably, without a hint of pathos.
“No, dear, I'm very, very happy,” Dorothea answered with fervour.
“All the better,” Celia thought. “But how strangely Dodo swings from one extreme to another.”
At lunch the next day, the butler handed Mr. Brooke something and said, “Jonas is back, sir. He brought this letter.”
Mr. Brooke read it, then nodded towards Dorothea. “Casaubon, my dear. He's coming to dinner. He didn't wait to write more—didn't wait, you know.”

There was nothing unusual in a dinner guest being announced to her sister in advance. But following her uncle's glance, Celia was struck by the peculiar effect on Dorothea. Something like a reflected white wing in sunlight seemed to sweep across her face, ending in one of her rare blushes. For the first time Celia wondered whether there might be more between Mr. Casaubon and her sister than his pleasure in learned conversation and hers in listening. Until now she had put Dorothea's admiration for this “ugly,” scholarly acquaintance in the same category as her admiration for Monsieur Liret at Lausanne, also ugly and learned. Dorothea had never tired of listening to old Monsieur Liret even when Celia's feet were freezing and the sight of the skin moving over his bald head had become positively dreadful. Why shouldn't her enthusiasm for Mr. Casaubon be of exactly the same kind? Besides, all learned men probably viewed young people rather as schoolmasters did.

Now, however, the suspicion flashing into Celia's mind truly startled her. Such surprises were rare: her extraordinary quickness at noticing certain kinds of signs usually prepared her for the outward events that interested her. She did not yet imagine Mr. Casaubon an accepted suitor. She had merely begun to feel disgust at the possibility of anything in Dorothea's mind tending that way. Here was something genuinely upsetting about Dodo. Refusing Sir James Chettam was all very well, but marrying Mr. Casaubon! Celia felt a kind of shame mixed with a sense of absurdity. Yet perhaps Dodo, if she really approached such extravagance, could be turned aside. Experience had often shown that one could count on her susceptibility to impressions. The day was damp, so they would not go walking. They went upstairs to their sitting room, where Celia noticed that instead of settling industriously to some occupation, Dorothea simply propped her elbow on an open book and gazed out at the great cedar, silvered by moisture. Celia herself began making a toy for the curate's children. She had no intention of rushing into any subject.

Dorothea was indeed thinking Celia ought to know how momentously Mr. Casaubon's position had changed since his last visit. It hardly seemed fair to leave her ignorant of something that must affect her manner towards him, yet she could not help shrinking from telling her. Dorothea blamed herself for a certain pettiness in this fear. She hated having small anxieties or schemes about her actions, but just now she was seeking the highest possible help against her dread of Celia's pretty, worldly-minded prose and its corrosive power. Her reverie broke, and the difficulty of deciding vanished, when Celia's small, rather throaty voice spoke in its usual tone of an aside, or a “by the way.”
“Is anyone coming to dinner apart from Mr. Casaubon?”
“Nobody that I've heard of.”
“I hope someone else is. Then I won't have to listen to him eating his soup like that.”
“What's so remarkable about the way he eats soup?”
“Really, Dodo, don't you hear him scraping his spoon? And he always blinks before he speaks. I don't know whether Locke blinked, but if he did, I'm certainly sorry for anyone sitting opposite him.”
“Celia,” Dorothea said with emphatic seriousness, “please don't make any more remarks like that.”
“Why shouldn't I? They're perfectly true,” Celia replied. She had reasons to persist, although she was beginning to feel afraid.
“Plenty of things are true that only the most commonplace minds notice.”

“Then commonplace minds must be rather useful. I think it's a pity Mr. Casaubon's mother wasn't more commonplace. She might have taught him better manners.” Having thrown this little spear, Celia felt frightened inside and ready to flee.
Dorothea's feelings had built into an avalanche; there was no possibility of further preparation.
“I ought to tell you, Celia, that Mr. Casaubon and I are engaged to be married.”

Perhaps Celia had never been so pale. Only her habitual care for anything in her hands saved the paper man she was making from an injured leg. She immediately set the fragile figure down and sat absolutely still for a few moments. A tear was forming when she spoke.
“Oh, Dodo, I hope you'll be happy.” At this moment her sisterly tenderness necessarily overcame her other feelings, and her fears arose from love.
Dorothea remained distressed and deeply hurt.
“So it's all settled?” Celia asked in a hushed, awed voice. “And does uncle know?”
“I've accepted Mr. Casaubon's proposal. Uncle brought me his letter, and he already knew what it contained.”

“Forgive me if I've said anything hurtful, Dodo,” Celia said with a small sob. She could never have imagined feeling as she did. The whole business had something of a funeral about it, with Mr. Casaubon as the officiating clergyman, whom it would be indecent to comment on.
“Never mind, Kitty. Don't be upset. We could never admire the same people. I often offend in much the same way; I tend to speak too harshly of people I don't like.”

Despite her generosity, Dorothea still smarted, perhaps as much at Celia's quiet astonishment as at her little criticisms. Naturally everyone around Tipton would be unsympathetic to the marriage. She knew nobody who shared her view of life and its highest purposes.

Nevertheless, before the evening ended she was very happy. During an hour's _tête-à-tête_ with Mr. Casaubon, she spoke more freely than ever, pouring out her joy at the prospect of devoting herself to him and learning how best to share and further his great aims. This childlike, unrestrained ardour moved him to an unfamiliar delight—what man would have been unmoved? He was not surprised to be its object—what lover would have been?

“My dear young lady—Miss Brooke—Dorothea!” he said, enclosing her hand in both of his. “This happiness exceeds anything I ever imagined might await me. I had never conceived of meeting someone whose mind and person united so richly the graces that could make marriage desirable. You possess all—more than all—the qualities I have always considered the distinctive virtues of womanhood. Your sex's greatest charm is its capacity for passionate, self-sacrificing affection; in this we recognize its fitness to round out and complete the existence of our own. Until now my pleasures have mostly been of the more austere kind: the satisfactions of a solitary scholar. I have had little inclination to gather flowers that would fade in my hand, but now I shall eagerly pick them to lay upon your breast.”

No speech could have been more honest in intention. Its chilly closing rhetoric was as sincere as a dog's bark or a courting rook's caw. Wouldn't it be rash to suppose there was no passion behind those sonnets to Delia that sound to us like a mandolin's thin music?

Dorothea's faith supplied everything his words left unstated. What believer finds a troubling omission or clumsy phrase? A prophet's or poet's text stretches to contain whatever we can put into it; even its bad grammar becomes sublime.

“I'm very ignorant. You'll be astonished at how little I know,” Dorothea said. “I have so many thoughts that may be entirely mistaken, and now I'll be able to tell you them all and ask you about them. But,” she added, quickly imagining how he might feel, “I won't trouble you too much—only when you want to listen. You must often be tired from pursuing your own subjects. It will be gain enough for me if you'll let me accompany you there.”

“How could I now continue along any path without your company?” Mr. Casaubon said, kissing her candid forehead and feeling heaven had bestowed a blessing exactly suited to his particular needs. Without knowing it, he was being influenced by the charm of a nature entirely free of hidden calculations, whether for immediate effect or distant purposes. That was what made Dorothea so childlike and, in some people's opinion, so foolish despite her reputed cleverness. Here, for example, she was figuratively throwing herself at Mr. Casaubon's feet and kissing his unfashionable shoe ties as if he were a Protestant Pope. She was doing nothing to teach him to wonder whether he deserved her; she merely asked herself anxiously how she could deserve him. Before he left the next day, they had agreed to marry within six weeks. Why wait? His house stood ready. It was no parsonage but a substantial mansion with extensive land. The curate lived in the parsonage and carried out every duty except preaching the morning sermon.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter VI
paragraphs:
My lady's tongue resembles meadow grass
That cuts the idle hand that strokes its blades.
Fine cutting is her trade: with spirit's edge
She splits a millet seed in two,
And makes economies no one can touch.

As Mr. Casaubon's carriage passed through the gateway, it blocked a small pony carriage driven by a lady with a servant behind her. Whether they recognized each other was uncertain: Mr. Casaubon gazed absently ahead, but the sharp-eyed lady managed a nod and a “How do you do?” just in time. Despite her shabby bonnet and very old Indian shawl, the deep curtsy with which the lodge keeper greeted the little carriage made clear that its occupant mattered.
“Well, Mrs. Fitchett, how are your hens laying these days?” asked the dark-eyed lady with the high colour, each word as sharply defined as carving.
“They lay well enough, ma'am, but they've taken to eating their eggs. I get no peace of mind with them at all.”
“Oh, the cannibals! Best sell them cheap at once. What would you take for a pair? One can't pay high prices to eat hens with bad characters.”
“Well, ma'am, half a crown. I couldn't let them go for less.”

“Half a crown, in these times! Come now—they're for the Rector's chicken broth on Sundays. He's eaten all of ours I can spare. Remember, Mrs. Fitchett, the sermon is half your payment. Take a pair of tumbler pigeons instead—little beauties. You must come and look at them. You haven't any tumblers among your pigeons.”
“Well, ma'am, Master Fitchett can come after work and look them over. He's keen on new breeds; he'll do it to oblige you.”
“Oblige me! It'll be the best bargain he ever made. A pair of church pigeons for two wicked Spanish hens that eat their own eggs! Just don't you and Fitchett boast too much, that's all!”

With these last words the carriage moved on, leaving Mrs. Fitchett laughing and slowly shaking her head, punctuating it with “Sure_ly_, sure_ly_!” One might infer that she would have found the countryside duller had the Rector's wife been less outspoken and less miserly. Indeed, farmers and labourers alike in Freshitt and Tipton would have been sadly short of conversation without stories of Mrs. Cadwallader's sayings and doings. Here was a lady of immeasurably lofty birth, descended, as it were, from earls unknown and dim as a crowd of heroic ghosts, who pleaded poverty, beat down prices and made jokes with perfect friendliness, yet a turn of speech that reminded you who she was. Such a woman made both rank and religion seem neighbourly, softening the bitterness of tithes still paid in kind. A far more exemplary person tinged with sour dignity would not have improved anyone's understanding of the Thirty-nine Articles, and would have done less to bind society together.
Mr. Brooke, who experienced Mrs. Cadwallader's virtues from another angle, winced a little when her name was announced in the library, where he sat alone.

“I see you've had our Lowick Cicero visiting,” she said, settling comfortably into a chair and throwing back her wraps to reveal a thin but well-proportioned figure. “I suspect the two of you are cooking up bad politics, or you wouldn't see so much of that lively gentleman. I shall report you. Remember, you're both suspect since you supported Peel over the Catholic Bill. I'll tell everyone you intend to stand for Middlemarch as a Whig when old Pinkerton resigns, and Casaubon will secretly help you: bribe the voters with pamphlets and open the public houses to hand them out. Come on, confess!”

“Nothing of the kind,” Mr. Brooke said, smiling and polishing his glasses, though the accusation really made him blush a little. “Casaubon and I hardly discuss politics. He doesn't much care about philanthropy—punishments and so on. Only Church questions interest him. Not my sphere of action, you know.”

“Ra-a-ther too much your sphere, my friend. I've heard what you've been up to. Who sold a piece of land to the Papists in Middlemarch? I believe you bought it for that purpose. You're a regular Guy Faux. See if they don't burn you in effigy this coming fifth of November. Humphrey wouldn't come and quarrel with you over it, so I've come myself.”
“Very well. I was ready to be persecuted for refusing to persecute—not persecuting, you know.”

“There you are! You've prepared that bit of claptrap for the election platform. Now _don't_ let them lure you onto the platform, my dear Mr. Brooke. A man always makes a fool of himself giving speeches. His only excuse is being on the right side, so he can ask a blessing on his hemming and hawing. You'll lose your way, I warn you. You'll make a Saturday leftovers pie of every party's opinions, and they'll all pelt you.”

“That's what I expect, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, unwilling to reveal how little he enjoyed this prophecy. “What I expect as an independent man. As for the Whigs, someone who follows the thinkers is unlikely to let any party hook him. He may go along with them up to a point—up to a certain point, you know. But that's what you ladies never understand.”

“Where your certain point is? No, indeed. I'd like someone to explain how a man without a party can have any fixed point, roaming about and never telling his friends his address. ‘Nobody knows where Brooke will be; you can't count on Brooke’—that's what people say about you, to be frank. Now, do become respectable. How will you enjoy going to the Sessions with everyone avoiding your eye, a bad conscience and an empty pocket?”

“I don't attempt to argue politics with a lady,” Mr. Brooke said with smiling unconcern, though he felt uncomfortably aware that this attack began the defensive campaign his rash actions had invited. “Your sex aren't thinkers, you know—_varium et mutabile semper_—that kind of thing. You don't know Virgil. I knew”—he remembered just in time that he had not personally met the Augustan poet—“I was going to say poor Stoddart, you know. That's what _he_ said. You ladies always oppose independence, a man caring only for truth and so on. And nowhere in the county are opinions narrower than here. I don't mean to throw stones, you know, but someone must take an independent line. If I don't, who will?”

“Who? Any upstart without family or position. People of standing should consume their independent nonsense at home, not hawk it round. And you, about to marry your niece, as good as your daughter, to one of our best men! Sir James would be terribly annoyed. It would be too hard on him if you turned yourself into a Whig signboard now.”

Again Mr. Brooke winced inwardly. The moment Dorothea's engagement was settled he had foreseen Mrs. Cadwallader's taunts. An ignorant observer might easily say, “Quarrel with Mrs. Cadwallader.” But where can a country gentleman go if he quarrels with his oldest neighbours? Who could appreciate the delicate flavour of the name Brooke if it were offered casually, like wine without a seal? Certainly a man can be cosmopolitan only up to a point.
“I hope Chettam and I will always be friends, but I'm sorry to say there's no prospect of his marrying my niece,” Mr. Brooke said, relieved to see through the window that Celia was coming in.
“Why ever not?” Mrs. Cadwallader asked, her voice sharp with surprise. “It can scarcely be two weeks since you and I were discussing it.”

“My niece has chosen another suitor—chosen him herself, you know. I had nothing to do with it. I'd have preferred Chettam; I'd have said any girl would choose him. But there's no accounting for these matters. Your sex is changeable, you know.”
“Why, who on earth are you saying you intend to let her marry?” Mrs. Cadwallader’s mind raced through all the possible choices open to Dorothea.

But Celia now entered, glowing from her garden walk, and the greetings spared Mr. Brooke an immediate reply. He stood hurriedly, said, “By the way, I must speak to Wright about the horses,” and shuffled quickly out.
“My dear child, what's all this about your sister being engaged?” Mrs. Cadwallader asked.
“She's engaged to Mr. Casaubon,” Celia replied, using her usual simplest statement of fact and welcoming this chance to speak alone with the Rector's wife.
“How frightful. How long has this been going on?”
“I only found out yesterday. The wedding is in six weeks.”
“Well, my dear, I wish you happiness in your brother-in-law.”
“I feel so sorry for Dorothea.”
“Sorry! Her own doing, I presume.”
“Yes. She says Mr. Casaubon possesses a great soul.”
“He's welcome to it.”
“Oh, Mrs. Cadwallader, I can't think it would be pleasant to marry a man with a great soul.”
“Well, my dear, let that be a warning. You know what one looks like now. When the next one asks to marry you, don't accept.”
“I'm quite certain I never would.”
“No, one in a family is plenty. So your sister never cared for Sir James Chettam? How would you have liked _him_ as a brother-in-law?”
“Very much. I'm sure he'd have made a good husband. Only,” Celia added with a faint blush—sometimes she seemed to blush as naturally as she breathed—“I don't think he'd have suited Dorothea.”
“Not lofty enough for her?”
“Dodo is terribly strict. She thinks so much about everything, and takes such care over what one says. Sir James never seemed able to please her.”
“I'm certain she must have encouraged him. That's not much to her credit.”
“Please don't be cross with Dodo. She doesn't notice things. She thought so much about the cottages, and sometimes she was rude to Sir James, but he's so kind he never took any notice.”

“Well,” Mrs. Cadwallader said, putting on her shawl and rising with apparent urgency, “I must go straight to Sir James and break the news. He'll have brought his mother home by now, and I must call. Your uncle will never tell him. We're all disappointed, my dear. Young people ought to consider their families when they marry. I set a bad example myself: married a poor clergyman and became an object of pity among the De Bracys, forced to scheme for my coal and pray to heaven for salad oil. Still, Casaubon has plenty of money; I'll grant him that. As for his blood, I suppose his family arms are three black cuttlefish and a commentator rampant. By the way, before I leave I must speak to your Mrs. Carter about pastry. I want my young cook to learn from her. Poor people with four children, like us, can't afford a good cook, you know. I'm sure Mrs. Carter will oblige me. Sir James's cook is an absolute dragon.”
Within the hour Mrs. Cadwallader had outmanoeuvred Mrs. Carter and driven to Freshitt Hall, near her own parsonage. Her husband lived at Freshitt and employed a curate at Tipton.

Sir James Chettam had returned from the short journey that had kept him away for two days. He had changed his clothes and meant to ride to Tipton Grange. His horse waited at the door as Mrs. Cadwallader arrived, and he immediately came out, whip in hand. Lady Chettam was not back yet, but Mrs. Cadwallader could not deliver her message before the grooms. She asked him to show her the new plants in the nearby conservatory. Once they had stopped to contemplate them, she said—
“I have a tremendous shock for you. I hope you're not as deeply in love as you claimed.”
There was no point objecting to Mrs. Cadwallader's way of expressing herself. Still, Sir James's face altered slightly. A vague alarm seized him.

“I do believe Brooke means to expose himself after all. I accused him of planning to stand for Middlemarch as a Liberal, and he looked foolish and never denied it. Talked about an independent line and the usual nonsense.”
“Is that everything?” Sir James asked with considerable relief.
“Why,” Mrs. Cadwallader retorted more sharply, “surely you wouldn't want him to become a public man in that fashion, turning himself into a kind of political Cheap Jack?”
“I imagine someone could talk him out of it. He wouldn't care for the expense.”

“That's what I told him. Reason can reach him there. There's always a grain or two of common sense in an ounce of stinginess. An excellent family trait, stinginess; it's the safe direction for madness to lean. And there must be a little crack in the Brooke family, or we wouldn't be seeing what we're about to see.”
“What, Brooke running for Middlemarch?”

“Something worse. I feel a little responsible, really. I always told you what a fine match Miss Brooke would make. I knew she had plenty of nonsense in her, a flighty sort of Methodist stuff. But girls grow out of these things. This time, though, I've been caught by surprise.”

“What do you mean, Mrs. Cadwallader?” Sir James asked. He feared Miss Brooke might have run away to join the Moravian Brethren or some ridiculous sect unknown in good society. The knowledge that Mrs. Cadwallader always made the worst of things partly reassured him. “What's happened to Miss Brooke? Please tell me plainly.”

“Very well. She's engaged.” Mrs. Cadwallader paused, watching the deep hurt on his face as he tried to conceal it with a nervous smile and tapped his boot with his whip. Soon she added, “To Casaubon.”
Sir James dropped his whip and bent to retrieve it. Perhaps his face had never concentrated so much disgust as when he turned back to her and repeated, “Casaubon?”
“Exactly. Now you know why I came.”
“Good God! How horrible! He's nothing but a mummy!” (Allowance must be made for the perspective of a flourishing but disappointed rival.)
“She says he's a great soul. A great bladder full of rattling dried peas!” Mrs. Cadwallader said.
“What right has an old bachelor like that to marry?” Sir James demanded. “He's already got one foot in the grave.”
“I suppose he intends to pull it back out.”
“Brooke shouldn't permit it. He ought to insist they wait until she comes of age. By then she'd think better of it. What else is a guardian for?”
“As though anyone could squeeze a firm decision out of Brooke!”
“Perhaps Cadwallader could speak to him.”

“Not him! Humphrey thinks everyone's delightful. I can never make him criticize Casaubon. He even speaks well of the bishop, though I tell him that's unnatural in a clergyman with a benefice. What can you do with a husband who so neglects propriety? I conceal it as best I can by criticizing everyone myself. Come, come, cheer up! You're well rid of Miss Brooke, a girl who'd expect you to see stars in daylight. Between ourselves, little Celia is worth two of her, and will probably be the better match after all. Marrying Casaubon is as good as entering a convent.”
“Oh, as for me—it's for Miss Brooke's sake that I think her friends ought to use their influence.”

“Well, Humphrey doesn't know yet. But when I tell him, depend on it, he'll say, ‘Why not? Casaubon's a good fellow—and young—young enough.’ These charitable people can't tell vinegar from wine until they've swallowed it and got colic. Still, if I were a man I'd prefer Celia, particularly once Dorothea had gone. The truth is, you've courted one and won the other. I can see she admires you almost as much as a man expects to be admired. From anyone but me you might think that an exaggeration. Goodbye!”

Sir James helped Mrs. Cadwallader into her carriage and then mounted his horse. His friend's unpleasant news would not deprive him of his ride. He would simply ride faster, in a direction away from Tipton Grange.

Now, why on earth should Mrs. Cadwallader concern herself with Miss Brooke's marriage? Why, once the match she liked to think she had helped arrange fell through, did she immediately lay the groundwork for another? Was there some clever plot, some furtive course of action a careful watcher with a telescope could uncover? Not at all. A telescope could have swept Tipton and Freshitt, the whole territory of her pony carriage, without detecting a suspicious meeting or any scene from which she returned with less than her usual undisturbed sharpness of eye and naturally high colour. Had that convenient vehicle existed in the time of the Seven Sages, one of them would surely have observed that following women in their pony carriages teaches you little about them. Even when we point a microscope at a drop of water, our interpretations turn out rather crude. Through a weak lens we may seem to see a creature displaying energetic greed as smaller creatures swim into it like so many animated tax pennies. A stronger lens reveals tiny hairs creating whirlpools for these victims, while the swallower waits passively at its tax office. In the same metaphorical way, a strong lens applied to Mrs. Cadwallader's matchmaking reveals minute causes at work, creating what we might call whirlpools of thought and speech that deliver the nourishment she needs. Her life had a simple country character, free from secrets foul, dangerous or otherwise important, and consciously untouched by the world's great affairs. Affairs in the great world therefore interested her all the more when letters from aristocratic relatives brought them: how fascinating younger sons had ruined themselves by marrying their mistresses; young Lord Tapir's fine, blue-blooded idiocy; old Lord Megatherium's furious, gouty tempers; the precise intersection of family trees that had carried a coronet to a fresh branch and extended scandal's connections. She retained every detail with complete accuracy and served them in an excellent pickle of epigrams. These pleased her the more because she believed in good birth and its absence as unquestioningly as in game and vermin. Poverty would never have made her disown anyone. A De Bracy reduced to eating dinner from a basin would have seemed a touching spectacle worth embellishing, and I fear his aristocratic vices would not have horrified her. Her feeling for the vulgar rich, however, approached religious hatred. They had probably made their money through high retail prices, and she hated high prices for anything not supplied to the Rectory as payment in kind. Such people had no place in God's design for the world, and their accents tormented the ears. A town full of these monsters was little more than low comedy, unworthy of inclusion in a well-bred scheme of the universe. Any lady tempted to judge Mrs. Cadwallader harshly should examine how comprehensive her own beautiful views are, and make quite sure they have room for every life honoured with existence alongside her own.

With a mind as active as phosphorus, biting everything nearby into its preferred shape, how could Mrs. Cadwallader consider the Miss Brookes and their marriage prospects no concern of hers? Especially when she had spent years scolding Mr. Brooke with friendly frankness and confidentially informing him that she thought him a poor creature. From the girls' arrival in Tipton she had arranged in advance Dorothea's marriage to Sir James. Had it happened, she would have been quite sure she had caused it. Its failure to happen after she had conceived it provoked an irritation every thinker can understand. She was the diplomat of Tipton and Freshitt, and anything happening against her plans was an offensive breach of order. She had no patience with whims like Miss Brooke's. She now realized that some of her husband's weak charitableness had infected her judgment of the girl: those Methodist fancies, that air of being more religious than rector and curate combined, came from a deeper, more ingrained disease than she had cared to believe.

“Still,” Mrs. Cadwallader told herself first and her husband later, “I wash my hands of her. If she'd married Sir James, she might have become a sane, sensible woman. He'd never have contradicted her, and without contradiction a woman has no reason to cling stubbornly to her absurdities. But now I wish her joy of her hair shirt.”

Naturally Mrs. Cadwallader had to choose another match for Sir James. Once she had made up her mind that it should be the younger Miss Brooke, she could scarcely have made a shrewder move towards her plan’s success than hinting to the baronet that he had touched Celia’s heart. He was not one of those gentlemen who pine after Sappho’s unreachable apple, laughing on the highest branch—those charms that

“Smile like a clump of cowslips on a cliff,
Beyond the reach of any willing hand.”

He had no sonnets to write, and could take no pleasure in discovering that the woman he preferred did not prefer him. The knowledge that Dorothea had chosen Mr. Casaubon had already bruised his attachment and loosened its grip. A sportsman he might be, but he felt differently about women than about grouse and foxes. He did not view his future wife as prey valued mainly for the excitement of pursuit. Nor was he so familiar with the customs of primitive peoples that he felt some symbolic combat for her, tomahawk in hand, necessary to preserve the historical continuity of marriage. Instead, he possessed the amiable vanity that draws us to people who like us and away from those who do not, along with a grateful, good nature. Merely imagining a woman's kindness towards him spun little threads of tenderness from his heart to hers.

So, after riding quite fast away from Tipton Grange for half an hour, Sir James slowed down and eventually turned onto a road offering a shorter route back. Various feelings combined to make him decide to visit the Grange that day after all, as though nothing had changed. He could not help feeling glad he had never proposed and been rejected. Ordinary friendly courtesy required him to call about the cottages; fortunately Mrs. Cadwallader had now prepared him to offer congratulations, if necessary, without excessive awkwardness. He truly disliked it: giving Dorothea up hurt badly. Yet deciding to make the visit immediately and master every outward sign of emotion offered a kind of teeth-gritting resistance, one irritation countering another. And although he did not clearly recognize the impulse, he certainly knew Celia would be there, and that he would pay her more attention than before.

We mortals, women and men alike, swallow plenty of disappointments between breakfast and dinner. We hold back tears, grow a little pale around the lips and answer questions with “Oh, nothing!” Pride helps us, and pride is no bad thing when it merely prompts us to hide our own wounds rather than wound other people.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter VII
paragraphs:
“Piacer e popone
Vuol la sua stagione.”
—_Italian Proverb_.

As one would expect, Mr. Casaubon spent much of these weeks at the Grange. Courtship interrupted work on his great project, the Key to all Mythologies, and naturally made him look forward all the more eagerly to courtship's happy conclusion. Still, he had knowingly accepted the interruption. He had decided the time had come to adorn his life with the graces of a woman's companionship, to brighten with feminine imagination the gloom that fatigue often spread over the intervals between scholarly labours, and to secure, at this summit of his life, the comfort of a woman's care for his declining years. Accordingly he resolved to surrender to the current of feeling, and perhaps was surprised to discover what a shallow trickle it was. As baptism by immersion can only be symbolic in drought-stricken regions, he found that sprinkling was the nearest his stream could bring him to a plunge. He concluded that poets greatly exaggerated the power of male passion. Nevertheless, he was pleased by Miss Brooke's fervent, submissive love, which promised to fulfil his most agreeable expectations of marriage. Once or twice he wondered whether some deficiency in Dorothea might explain the moderation of his surrender. But he could identify none, nor imagine a woman who would please him better. Clearly, then, he had no explanation left except the exaggerations handed down in human tradition.

“Couldn't I start preparing now to be more useful?” Dorothea asked him one morning early in their engagement. “Could I learn to read Latin and Greek aloud to you, like Milton's daughters reading to their father without understanding the words?”

“I fear you would find it tiring,” Mr. Casaubon answered with a smile. “Indeed, if I recall correctly, the young women you mention considered this exercise in unfamiliar languages a reason to rebel against the poet.”

“Yes, but first they were very naughty girls, or they'd have been proud to serve such a father. And second, they could have studied privately and taught themselves to understand what they read. Then it would have interested them. I hope you don't expect me to be naughty and stupid?”

“I expect you to be everything an exquisite young lady can be in every possible relation of life. Certainly your ability to copy Greek letters could be very useful. With that purpose, beginning with a little reading would be advisable.”

Dorothea seized on this permission as a precious gift. She would not have immediately asked him to teach her the languages, fearing above all to be a burden rather than a help. But devotion to her future husband was not her sole reason for wanting Latin and Greek. These territories of male knowledge seemed to offer a vantage point from which every truth could be seen more truly. As things stood, awareness of her ignorance made her constantly question her own conclusions. How could she be sure that one-room cottages did not glorify God, when men who knew the classics appeared able to combine indifference to cottages with zeal for that glory? Perhaps even Hebrew was necessary—at least its alphabet and a few roots—to get to the heart of things and judge a Christian's social duties correctly. She had not yet reached the degree of self-renunciation at which having a wise husband would satisfy her. Poor child, she wanted to be wise herself. For all her supposed cleverness, Miss Brooke was certainly naive. Celia, whose mind nobody considered particularly powerful, recognized the emptiness of other people's pretensions far more readily. Feeling little in general seems the only safeguard against feeling too much on any particular occasion.

Nevertheless, Mr. Casaubon agreed to spend an hour at a time listening and teaching, like a schoolmaster with small boys—or rather like a lover, to whom his beloved's elementary ignorance and difficulties seem touchingly appropriate. Few scholars would have objected to teaching the alphabet in such circumstances. Dorothea herself, however, felt somewhat shocked and discouraged by her own slowness. The answers to her timid questions about the purpose of Greek accents raised a painful suspicion that this subject might indeed contain secrets beyond a woman's powers of understanding.
On that point Mr. Brooke had no doubts. One day, entering the library during a reading lesson, he expressed himself with his customary force.
“Well, but Casaubon, deep studies like this—classics, mathematics and all that—strain a woman too much. Too much of a strain, you know.”
“Dorothea is only learning to read the letters,” Mr. Casaubon said, avoiding the issue. “She very thoughtfully proposed to spare my eyes.”

“Ah, well, without understanding, you know—that might not be so bad. But the feminine mind has a lightness, a touch-and-go quality. Music, the fine arts, that sort of thing—women should study those up to a point, but lightly, you know. A woman ought to be able to sit down and play or sing you a fine old English tune. That's what I like, though I've heard most things. Been to the opera in Vienna: Gluck, Mozart, everything of that sort. But I'm conservative about music. It isn't like ideas, you know. I stay with the good old tunes.”

“Mr. Casaubon doesn't like the piano, and I'm very glad of it,” said Dorothea. Her low opinion of domestic music and ladies' fine arts deserves forgiveness when we consider the faint tinkling and daubing that chiefly made them up in that dark age. She smiled gratefully up at her fiancé. Had he kept asking her to play “The Last Rose of Summer,” she would have needed great resignation. “He says there's only an old harpsichord at Lowick, and it's covered in books.”

“Ah, my dear, there Celia has the advantage. She plays very prettily and is always willing. Still, if Casaubon doesn't like it, you're all right. But it's a pity to lack these little recreations, Casaubon. Keeping the bow strung all the time—that sort of thing, you know—won't do.”

“I have never found recreation in having my ears tormented by rhythmic noises,” Mr. Casaubon said. “A frequently repeated tune has the absurd effect of forcing the words in my mind into a kind of minuet to keep time. After boyhood, I imagine, such an effect is barely tolerable. I say nothing of the grander forms of music, worthy of accompanying solemn ceremonies and even, in the ancient conception, of exercising an educational influence. Those do not immediately concern us here.”
“No, but I would enjoy music of that kind,” Dorothea said. “On our way home from Lausanne, uncle took us to hear the great organ at Freiberg, and it made me sob.”
“That isn't healthy, my dear,” Mr. Brooke said. “Casaubon, she'll be in your hands now. You must teach my niece to take things more calmly. Eh, Dorothea?”
He ended with a smile, not wanting to hurt her. He did think, though, that since she refused to consider Chettam, perhaps an early marriage to someone as sober as Casaubon was best.

“Remarkable, all the same,” he told himself as he shuffled out. “Remarkable that she should have liked him. But it's a good match. I'd have exceeded my responsibilities by preventing it, whatever Mrs. Cadwallader says. Casaubon is almost certain to become a bishop. That pamphlet of his on the Catholic Question came at just the right moment. A deanery, at least. They owe him a deanery.”

Here I must establish my claim to philosophical reflection by observing that Mr. Brooke, on this occasion, little imagined the Radical speech he would later be led to make about bishops' incomes. What elegant historian would miss a striking opportunity to point out that his heroes failed to foresee world history, or even their own actions? For instance, that Henry of Navarre, as a Protestant infant, scarcely thought of becoming a Catholic king; or that Alfred the Great, timing his laborious nights with burning candles, never imagined future gentlemen measuring their idle days with watches. Here is a mine of truth which, however vigorously excavated, will probably outlast our coal.

But I will add something about Mr. Brooke with perhaps less historical precedent: even if he had foreseen his speech, it might have made little difference. Enjoying the thought of his niece's husband drawing a large Church income was one thing; delivering a Liberal speech was another. A mind that cannot view a subject from several angles is a narrow one.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter VIII
paragraphs:
“Oh, save her! I am her brother now,
And you her father. Every gentle girl
Should find a guardian in every gentleman.”

Sir James Chettam was surprised how much he still enjoyed visiting the Grange once he had faced the first difficulty of seeing Dorothea as a woman engaged to someone else. Naturally, forked lightning seemed to shoot through him when he first approached her, and throughout the visit he knew he was concealing distress. Yet good as he was, we must admit that he suffered less than he would have if he had considered his rival a brilliant and desirable match. He did not feel eclipsed by Mr. Casaubon, only shocked that Dorothea laboured under a sad delusion. Compassion mingled with his humiliation and took away some of its bitterness.

Still, though Sir James told himself he had entirely given her up—since, with Desdemona's perversity, she had rejected a prospective match so plainly suitable and natural—he could not yet passively accept her engagement to Mr. Casaubon. The first day he saw them together with his new knowledge, he felt he had not taken the matter seriously enough. Brooke was truly at fault; he ought to have prevented it. Who could speak to him? Perhaps even now something could be done, at least to postpone the wedding. On the way home he turned into the Rectory and asked for Mr. Cadwallader. Fortunately the Rector was in. Sir James was shown into the study, where all the fishing tackle hung. Mr. Cadwallader himself was working at his lathe in a small adjoining room and called him through. These two were closer friends than any other landowner and clergyman in the county, a significant fact in keeping with the kindly expressions on their faces.

Mr. Cadwallader was a large man with full lips and a sweet smile, very plain and rough-looking, but possessed of an unshakeable ease and good humour that spread to those around him. Like great grassy hills in sunlight, they soothed even an irritated self-importance and made it a little ashamed. “Well, how are you?” he asked, showing a hand not quite fit to shake. “Sorry I missed you earlier. Anything particular? You look annoyed.”
A small crease marked Sir James's brow, a slight lowering of the eyebrows that he seemed deliberately to deepen as he replied.
“It's just this behaviour of Brooke's. I really believe someone ought to speak to him.”

“What, his plan to stand for Parliament?” Mr. Cadwallader asked, continuing to arrange the reels he had just made on the lathe. “I doubt he means it. But where's the harm if he wants to? Anyone opposed to the Whigs should be glad they aren't putting forward their strongest man. They won't knock down the Constitution using our friend Brooke's head as a battering ram.”

“Oh, I don't mean that,” Sir James said. He had put his hat down and dropped into a chair, where he clasped his leg and bitterly examined the sole of his boot. “I mean this marriage. Letting that lovely young girl marry Casaubon.”
“What's wrong with Casaubon? I know no harm of him, if the girl likes him.”

“She's too young to know what she likes. Her guardian should intervene. He shouldn't let it be rushed through like this. I'm surprised a man like you, Cadwallader, a man with daughters, can regard it indifferently—and with your kind heart! Do consider it seriously.”

“I'm not joking. I couldn't be more serious,” the Rector said with an irritating little inward chuckle. “You're as bad as Elinor. She's been urging me to lecture Brooke, and I've reminded her that her friends thought very poorly of her own match when she married me.”
“But look at Casaubon,” Sir James protested indignantly. “He must be fifty, and I doubt he's ever been much more than a man's shadow. Just look at his legs!”

“Damn you handsome young fellows! You expect everything in the world to go your way. You don't understand women. They admire you half as much as you admire yourselves. Elinor used to tell her sisters she'd married me for my ugliness: it was so varied and entertaining it overcame all her prudence.”
“You! Loving you would be easy for any woman. But looks aren't the issue. I don't _like_ Casaubon.” This was Sir James's strongest way of suggesting a poor opinion of someone's character.
“Why? What do you know against him?” The Rector set down his reels and hooked his thumbs into his waistcoat armholes, looking attentive.
Sir James hesitated. Explaining his reasons was seldom easy for him. Since he felt only what was reasonable, it seemed strange that other people should need to be told. At last he said—
“Come now, Cadwallader, does he have any heart?”

“Well, yes. Not a melting one, I don't mean that, but a sound core—you can rely on _that_. He's very good to his poor relations. He pays pensions to several of the women and spends a good deal educating a young man. Casaubon lives by his sense of justice. His mother's sister married badly—a Pole, I think—and lost her place in society; anyway, her family disowned her. Without that, Casaubon wouldn't have half so much money. I believe he sought his cousins out himself to see what he could do. Not every man would ring as true as that if you tested his metal. _You_ would, Chettam, but not everyone.”

“I don't know,” Sir James said, reddening. “I'm not so certain of myself.” After a pause he added, “Casaubon did the right thing there. But a man can want to act rightly and still be a sort of legal code on parchment. A woman might not be happy with him. And when a girl is as young as Miss Brooke, I think her friends should intervene a little to keep her from doing something foolish. You're laughing because you imagine I'm thinking of myself. But on my honour, that isn't it. I'd feel exactly the same if I were her brother or her uncle.”
“Well, then, what would you actually do?”
“I'd insist the marriage couldn't be settled until she came of age. And believe me, in that case it would never happen. I wish you saw it my way. I wish you'd talk to Brooke.”

Sir James stood as he finished, seeing Mrs. Cadwallader enter from the study. She held her youngest daughter's hand. The child, about five, ran straight to papa, who settled her comfortably on his knee.

“I can hear what you're discussing,” his wife said. “But you won't influence Humphrey. As long as the fish take his bait, everyone is exactly as they should be. Bless you, Casaubon owns a trout stream and doesn't want to fish it himself. Could anyone be a better fellow?”
“Well, there's something to that,” the Rector said with his quiet inward laugh. “Owning a trout stream is a very good quality in a man.”
“But seriously,” Sir James persisted, his irritation still unspent, “don't you think the Rector might help if he spoke up?”
“Oh, I warned you what he'd say,” Mrs. Cadwallader answered, raising her eyebrows. “I've done what I can. I wash my hands of this marriage.”

“First of all,” the Rector said, becoming rather serious, “it would be absurd to expect me to convince Brooke and get him to act on it. He's a very good fellow, but soft as pulp. He'll flow into any mould, but he won't hold the shape.”
“He might hold it long enough to postpone the wedding,” Sir James replied.

“But my dear Chettam, why should I use my influence against Casaubon unless I were far more certain than I am that it would benefit Miss Brooke? I know nothing bad about him. His Xisuthrus and Fee-fo-fum and all the rest don't interest me, but then my fishing tackle doesn't interest him. His position on the Catholic Question surprised me, but he's always been civil, and I see no reason to spoil his sport. For all I know, Miss Brooke could be happier with him than with any other man.”
“Humphrey! You try my patience. You know perfectly well you'd rather eat dinner under a hedge than alone with Casaubon. You've nothing to say to each other.”
“What has that to do with Miss Brooke marrying him? She isn't doing it to entertain me.”
“There isn't any healthy red blood in his body,” Sir James declared.
“No. Someone examined a drop through a magnifying glass and found nothing but semicolons and parentheses,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied.
“Why doesn't he publish his book instead of getting married?” Sir James asked, with a disgust he considered justified by an English layman's sound instincts.

“Oh, he dreams in footnotes, and they carry off all his brains. They say he made an abstract of ‘Hop o' my Thumb’ as a little boy, and he's been making abstracts ever since. Ugh! And Humphrey keeps saying a woman could be happy with that man.”
“Well, Miss Brooke likes him,” said the Rector. “I don't claim to understand every young lady's preferences.”
“But suppose she was your own daughter?” Sir James asked.

“Then it would be different. She _isn't_ my daughter, and I don't feel obliged to interfere. Casaubon's as good as most of us. He's a learned clergyman who does credit to his profession. Some Radical making a speech in Middlemarch called him the incumbent who chopped learned straw, Freke the bricks-and-mortar incumbent, and me the fishing incumbent. On my word, I can't see that one is better or worse than another.” The Rector finished with his silent chuckle. He always appreciated the joke in satire directed at himself. Like the rest of him, his conscience was large and comfortable: it did only what caused it no trouble.

Plainly Mr. Cadwallader would not obstruct Miss Brooke's marriage. Sir James sadly felt she was to have complete freedom to misjudge. His good nature showed in the fact that he never slackened his intention to carry out Dorothea's cottage scheme. Doubtless persistence best preserved his dignity, but pride only helps us act generously; it no more creates generosity than vanity creates wit. Dorothea now understood enough of his feelings to value the integrity with which he continued a landlord's duty first undertaken from a lover's eagerness to please. Her pleasure in it was strong enough to matter even amid her present happiness. Perhaps Sir James's cottages received all the interest she could spare from Mr. Casaubon—or rather from the symphony of hopeful dreams, admiring trust and passionate devotion that the learned gentleman had set playing in her soul. Thus, on later visits, while the good baronet began offering Celia small attentions, he found himself talking to Dorothea with increasing pleasure. She was now entirely relaxed and free from irritation with him. Gradually he discovered the delight of candid kindness and companionship between a man and woman who have no passion either to conceal or confess.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter IX
paragraphs:
1st Gentleman. An ancient country, ancient oracles
Called “thirsty for law”: its every struggle sought
Order and perfect governance.
Tell me, where are such countries now? . . .
2nd Gentleman. Where they always were—in human souls.

Mr. Brooke found Mr. Casaubon's conduct over the marriage settlements entirely satisfactory. The preparations moved smoothly forward, making the weeks of courtship seem shorter. The bride-to-be must visit her future home and specify whatever changes she wanted. A woman gives orders before marriage to develop an appetite for obedience afterwards. Certainly the mistakes we mortals, male and female, make when allowed our own way might reasonably cause surprise that we enjoy it so much.

On a grey but dry November morning, Dorothea drove to Lowick with her uncle and Celia. Mr. Casaubon lived in the manor house. Nearby, visible from parts of the garden, stood the little church, opposite the old parsonage. At the beginning of his career he had held only the parish living, but his brother's death had given him the manor too. Its small park contained fine old oaks here and there, and an avenue of lime trees approached the south-west front. A sunken fence divided park from pleasure grounds, so the drawing-room windows offered an uninterrupted view down a grassy slope, past the limes, into level cornfields and pasture that often seemed to dissolve into a lake beneath the setting sun. This was the house's happy side. The south and east looked rather mournful even on the brightest morning. There the grounds were more cramped, the flower beds poorly tended, and large clumps of trees, mostly gloomy yews, rose high less than ten yards from the windows. Built of greenish stone in the old English style, the house was not ugly, but its small windows gave it a melancholy look. It was the sort of place that needed children, abundant flowers, open windows and little glimpses of bright things to appear a joyful home. In this late autumn, with a few remaining yellow leaves drifting across dark evergreens in sunless stillness, the house itself seemed in autumnal decline. When Mr. Casaubon appeared, he had no bloom for such a background to emphasize.

“Oh dear!” Celia thought. “I'm sure Freshitt Hall would have been nicer.” She imagined its white freestone, columned porch and flower-filled terrace, with Sir James smiling above the flowers like a prince emerging from enchantment in a rosebush, his handkerchief newly transformed from its sweetest petals. Sir James, who talked so agreeably, always of sensible things and never of scholarship! Celia possessed the light, youthful feminine tastes that solemn, weather-beaten gentlemen sometimes prefer in wives. Fortunately Mr. Casaubon's preference was different, since he would have had no chance with her.

Dorothea, by contrast, found everything she could wish for in house and grounds. The dark shelves in the long library, carpets and curtains faded by time, odd old maps and bird's-eye views along the corridor walls, with an antique vase here and there beneath them—none oppressed her. They seemed more cheerful than the casts and pictures at the Grange, brought home by her uncle from his long-ago travels, probably among the ideas he had once absorbed. To poor Dorothea those austere classical nudes and simpering Renaissance-Correggio effects were painfully inexplicable, staring into the heart of her Puritan view of things. Nobody had taught her how to connect them with her own life. Lowick's owners apparently had not travelled, and Mr. Casaubon's studies of the past did not employ such aids.

Dorothea explored the house with delighted feeling. Everything seemed sacred. This would be the home of her married life. Whenever Mr. Casaubon drew attention to some particular arrangement and asked if she wanted it changed, she looked up at him with complete trust. She received each appeal to her taste gratefully, but saw nothing to alter. His painstaking courtesy and formal tenderness seemed flawless. Every blank she filled with unseen perfections, interpreting him as she interpreted Providence, blaming apparent discords on her own inability to hear the higher harmonies. Courtship leaves many such blanks for loving faith to fill with happy certainty.

“Now, my dear Dorothea, please do me the favour of choosing which room you would like for your private sitting room,” Mr. Casaubon said, showing that his conception of feminine nature was broad enough to accommodate this need.

“It's very kind of you to think of it,” Dorothea replied, “but I assure you I'd rather have all such matters decided for me. I'd be much happier with everything just as it is, the way you're used to it, or whatever arrangement you choose yourself. I have no reason to wish for anything else.”
“Oh, Dodo,” Celia said, “why not have the upstairs room with the bow window?”

Mr. Casaubon led them there. The bow window looked down the lime avenue. All the furnishings were faded blue, and a cluster of miniature portraits showed ladies and gentlemen with powdered hair. A tapestry above a door displayed another blue-green world, with a pale stag in it. The slender-legged chairs and tables looked easy to knock over. One could imagine a tightly laced lady's ghost returning to the scene of her embroidery. A light bookcase holding small calf-bound volumes of polite literature completed the room.
“Yes,” Mr. Brooke said, “this would be pretty with new curtains and sofas and that sort of thing. It's a little bare at present.”

“No, uncle,” Dorothea said eagerly. “Please don't suggest changing anything. So much else in the world needs changing; I'd like to accept these things as they are. And you like them as they are, don't you?” she added, looking at Mr. Casaubon. “Perhaps it was your mother's room when she was young.”
“It was indeed,” he replied, bending his head slowly.
“This is your mother,” Dorothea said, turning to study the miniatures. “It's like the tiny portrait you brought me, though I'd think it a better likeness. And the one opposite—who is she?”
“Her older sister. Like you and your sister, they were their parents' only children. Their parents' portraits hang above, as you see.”

“The sister is pretty,” Celia remarked, implying less approval of Mr. Casaubon's mother. It opened a new prospect to her imagination that he belonged to a family whose members had all once been young, the ladies wearing necklaces.

“It's an unusual face,” Dorothea said, examining it closely. “Those deep grey eyes set rather close together, and the delicate, irregular nose with a sort of ripple in it, and all the powdered curls falling backwards. Altogether I'd call her unusual rather than pretty. She doesn't even have a family resemblance to your mother.”
“No. Their fortunes were not alike either.”
“You haven't told me about her,” Dorothea said.
“My aunt made an unfortunate marriage. I never met her.”

Dorothea wondered a little, but felt it would be tactless just then to ask for details he did not volunteer. She turned to admire the view through the window. The sun had recently broken through the grey, and the lime avenue cast shadows.
“Could we walk in the garden now?” Dorothea asked.

“And you'll want to see the church, you know,” Mr. Brooke said. “A curious little church. And the village. It's all tucked into a nutshell. It will suit you, Dorothea, by the way. The cottages look like a row of almshouses—little gardens, gillyflowers, that kind of thing.”
“Yes, please,” Dorothea said, looking at Mr. Casaubon. “I'd like to see all of it.” His most vivid description of Lowick's cottages so far had been that they were “not bad.”

Soon they followed a gravel path running mostly between grassy edges and clumps of trees, the shortest route to the church, Mr. Casaubon said. At the small churchyard gate they stopped while he went to the nearby parsonage for a key. Celia had lagged behind, but came forward when she saw he had gone. In her easy, clipped way, which always seemed to deny any suspicion of malice, she said—
“Do you know, Dorothea, I saw someone quite young coming along one of the paths.”
“Is that so surprising, Celia?”
“There might be a young gardener, you know—why not?” Mr. Brooke suggested. “I told Casaubon he ought to change his gardener.”
“No, it wasn't a gardener,” Celia said. “A gentleman with a sketchbook. He had light brown curls. I only saw him from behind, but he was quite young.”
“The curate's son, perhaps,” Mr. Brooke said. “Ah, Casaubon's coming back with Tucker. He's going to introduce him. You haven't met Tucker yet.”

Mr. Tucker was the middle-aged curate, one of the “inferior clergy,” who generally have no shortage of sons. But after the introduction nothing in the conversation prompted a question about his family, and everyone except Celia forgot the startling appearance of youth. She privately refused to believe that those light brown curls and that slender figure could be related to Mr. Tucker, who looked exactly as old and musty as she would have expected Mr. Casaubon's curate to look. Doubtless he was an excellent man destined for heaven—Celia did not wish to lack principle—but the corners of his mouth were so unpleasant. She rather gloomily imagined her time at Lowick as bridesmaid, while the curate probably had no pretty little children she could like without reference to principle.

Mr. Tucker proved invaluable on the walk; perhaps Mr. Casaubon had foreseen this. The curate answered all Dorothea's questions about the villagers and other parishioners. Everyone in Lowick was comfortable, he assured her. Every tenant of those low-rent paired cottages kept a pig, and the strips of back garden were well maintained. The little boys wore excellent corduroy; the girls became tidy servants or did some straw plaiting at home. There were no looms, no religious Dissent. Though people generally preferred saving money to cultivating spirituality, vice was rare. Speckled hens were so numerous that Mr. Brooke observed, “I see your farmers leave some barley for the women to glean. The poor here could have a chicken in the pot, as that good French king wished for all his people. The French eat plenty of chickens—scrawny chickens, you know.”
“I think that was a very cheap wish,” Dorothea said indignantly. “Are kings such monsters that a wish like that counts as a royal virtue?”
“And if he wished them a scrawny chicken,” Celia added, “that wouldn't be nice. But perhaps he wanted them to have fat ones.”

“Yes, but that word has vanished from the text, or perhaps was subauditum—that is, present in the king's mind but unspoken,” Mr. Casaubon said, smiling and inclining his head towards Celia. She immediately fell back a little, unable to bear his blinking at her.

Dorothea became silent on the return to the house. She felt disappointed, and ashamed of the disappointment, that Lowick offered her nothing to do. For a few minutes she considered how much she would have preferred discovering that her future home lay in a parish with a greater share of the world's misery, where she could take on more active duties. Then, returning to the future actually before her, she pictured a more complete devotion to Mr. Casaubon's aims, while she waited for new responsibilities. The higher knowledge their companionship would give her might reveal many.
Mr. Tucker soon left: parish work prevented him from lunching at the Hall. As they passed through the little gate into the garden again, Mr. Casaubon said—
“You seem somewhat sad, Dorothea. I hope what you have seen has pleased you.”

“I feel something perhaps foolish and wrong,” she replied with her usual candour. “Almost wishing people here needed more help. I've known so few ways of making my life useful at all. Naturally my ideas of usefulness must be narrow. I need to learn new ways to help people.”
“Undoubtedly,” Mr. Casaubon replied. “Every position brings its appropriate duties. I trust yours as mistress of Lowick will leave none of your aspirations unsatisfied.”
“I do believe that,” Dorothea said earnestly. “Please don't think I'm unhappy.”
“That is good. But if you are not tired, let us return to the house by a different route from the one we took before.”

Dorothea was not tired at all. They took a short detour towards a fine yew, the chief inherited glory of the grounds on this side. Approaching it, they saw a figure seated on a bench sketching the old tree, conspicuous against the dark evergreens. Walking ahead with Celia, Mr. Brooke turned and asked—
“Who's that young man, Casaubon?”
They were quite close by the time Mr. Casaubon replied—
“A young relation of mine, a second cousin. In fact,” he added, looking at Dorothea, “he is the grandson of my aunt Julia, the lady whose portrait you were examining.”
The young man put down his sketchbook and stood. His abundant light brown curls and youthful appearance immediately identified him as the figure Celia had seen.
“Dorothea, may I introduce my cousin, Mr. Ladislaw? Will, this is Miss Brooke.”

He was close enough now that when he lifted his hat, Dorothea saw grey eyes set rather near together, a fine irregular nose with a little ripple, and hair falling backwards. His mouth and chin, however, were more pronounced and challenging than those in his grandmother's miniature. Young Ladislaw apparently felt no need to smile as if delighted to meet his future second cousin by marriage and her relations. He wore instead a rather sulky expression of discontent.
“You're an artist, I see,” Mr. Brooke said, picking up the sketchbook and leafing through it with his usual lack of ceremony.
“No, I only do a little sketching. There's nothing there worth seeing,” young Ladislaw said, reddening, perhaps from annoyance rather than modesty.

“Oh, come, here's a nice bit. I used to do a little of this myself, you know. Now look here: this is what I call a nice thing, done with what we used to call _brio_.” He held out to the girls a large coloured sketch of rocky ground, trees and a pool.

“I'm no judge of such things,” Dorothea said, not coldly but eagerly protesting the appeal to her opinion. “You know, uncle, I never see the beauty in those pictures you tell me everyone praises. They're a language I don't understand. I suppose there's a connection between pictures and nature that I'm too ignorant to feel, just as you can see the meaning of a Greek sentence that says nothing to me.” She looked up at Mr. Casaubon, who inclined his head, while Mr. Brooke smiled casually and said—

“Bless me, how different people are! But you were taught badly, you know. Otherwise this is just the thing for girls—sketching, fine art and so forth. Instead you took to drawing plans. You don't understand _morbidezza_ and that sort of thing. I hope you'll visit me and let me show you what I used to do in this line,” he continued, turning to Ladislaw, whose absorbed scrutiny of Dorothea had to be interrupted. Ladislaw had decided she must be an unpleasant girl, since she was marrying Casaubon. Even had he believed her professed stupidity about pictures, it would have confirmed his opinion. Instead, he heard a concealed criticism and felt sure she thought his sketch dreadful. Her apology was too clever: she was mocking both him and her uncle. But what a voice! Like the voice of a soul that had once inhabited an Aeolian harp. Nature must be inconsistent here. A girl capable of marrying Casaubon could have no passion of any kind. Still, he turned away and bowed his thanks for Mr. Brooke's invitation.

“We'll look through my Italian engravings together,” the good-natured man continued. “I've endless things like that, put away for years. One gets rusty in this part of the country, you know. Not you, Casaubon; you stick to your studies. But my best ideas get buried at the bottom, fall out of use, you know. You clever young men must watch out for laziness. I was too lazy myself; otherwise there was a time when I might have been anywhere.”
“A timely warning,” Mr. Casaubon said. “But we should go on to the house now, in case the young ladies are tired of standing.”

Once their backs were turned, Ladislaw sat down to resume his sketch. Amusement spread over his face as he worked, until finally he threw back his head and laughed aloud. Partly the reception of his artistic effort entertained him, partly the idea of his solemn cousin as that girl's lover, and partly Mr. Brooke's description of the position he might have reached but for laziness. Mr. Will Ladislaw's sense of absurdity lit his face very pleasantly. It was sheer enjoyment of the comic, without a trace of sneering or self-importance.
“What's your nephew going to do with himself, Casaubon?” Mr. Brooke asked as they continued walking.
“You mean my cousin, not my nephew.”
“Yes, yes, your cousin. But what career, you know?”

“The answer is painfully uncertain. After Rugby he refused an English university, where I would gladly have sent him, and chose what I must consider the irregular course of studying at Heidelberg. Now he wants to go abroad again without any definite aim beyond a vague intention of what he calls culture: preparation for he knows not what. He refuses to choose a profession.”
“I suppose he has no income except what you supply.”

“I have always led him and his friends to understand that I would provide, within reason, what was needed for a scholarly education and a respectable start in life. I am therefore obliged to fulfil the expectations I created,” Mr. Casaubon said, presenting his behaviour as a matter of simple duty. Dorothea admired this delicacy.
“He's eager to travel. Perhaps he'll become a Bruce or a Mungo Park,” Mr. Brooke suggested. “I once had some idea of that myself.”

“No, he has no inclination to explore or to expand our geognosis, our knowledge of the earth. That would be a definite aim I could approve to some extent, though I would not congratulate him on choosing a career so often ending in an early, violent death. Far from wishing for more precise knowledge of the earth's surface, he says he would rather not know the Nile's sources. He thinks some unexplored regions should remain as hunting grounds for the poetic imagination.”
“Well, there's something to be said for that, you know,” Mr. Brooke remarked, with an undeniably impartial mind.

“I fear it is merely another expression of his general imprecision and unwillingness to be thorough about anything. That would bode poorly in any profession, secular or sacred, even if he submitted to ordinary rules sufficiently to choose one.”

“Perhaps he has conscientious doubts about his own fitness,” Dorothea suggested, interested in finding a favourable explanation. “Law and medicine ought to be very serious professions to enter, shouldn't they? People's lives and fortunes depend on them.”

“Certainly. But I fear my young relation Will Ladislaw chiefly dislikes these professions because he dislikes steady application, and the learning that serves as a necessary tool without being charming or immediately appealing to a self-indulgent taste. I have emphasized to him Aristotle's admirably concise observation: to accomplish any work regarded as a goal, one must first exercise many lesser powers or acquired skills, and that requires patience. I have shown him my manuscript volumes, the product of years of labour in preparation for a work still unfinished. It has been useless. He answers careful reasoning of this sort by calling himself Pegasus, and every kind of assigned work ‘harness.’”
Celia laughed. It surprised her to discover that Mr. Casaubon could say something genuinely amusing.
“Well, you know, he might turn out another Byron, Chatterton or Churchill, something of that sort. There's no telling,” Mr. Brooke said. “Will you let him go to Italy, or wherever he wants?”
“Yes. I have agreed to give him a modest allowance for a year or so. He asks no more. I shall let freedom put him to the test.”

“That's very kind of you,” Dorothea said, looking up at him with delight. “It's noble. After all, people may have a calling within them that they don't yet clearly understand, mayn't they? Perhaps they seem idle and weak because they're still growing. I think we should be very patient with one another.”
“I suppose being engaged has taught you that patience is good,” Celia said as soon as they were alone, taking off their outdoor things.
“You mean I'm very impatient, Celia.”
“Yes, when people don't say and do exactly what you want.” Since the engagement, Celia had become less afraid of “saying things” to Dorothea. Cleverness seemed more pitiable to her than ever.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter X
paragraphs: “He would have caught a dreadful cold if his only clothes had been the skin of a bear that had not yet been killed.”—FULLER.

Young Ladislaw never made the visit Mr. Brooke had invited him to pay. Only six days later Mr. Casaubon said his young relation had left for the Continent, with a chilly vagueness that seemed intended to discourage questions. Indeed, Will had refused to name any destination more precise than the whole of Europe. Genius, he maintained, necessarily resented restraints. On the one hand it needed complete freedom for spontaneous expression; on the other, it could confidently await the universe's summons to its particular task, merely keeping itself receptive to every sublime possibility. There are many postures of receptivity, and Will had sincerely tried several. He was not especially fond of wine but had drunk too much on several occasions simply to experiment with that form of ecstasy. He had fasted until faint, then eaten lobster for supper; he had made himself sick with opium. Nothing very original resulted. Opium convinced him only that his constitution differed completely from De Quincey's. The additional circumstance that would bring genius into being had not arrived; the universe had yet to beckon. Even Caesar's destiny was once no more than a magnificent foreboding. We know what a masquerade development can be, what powerful forms may hide inside helpless embryos. The world, in fact, overflows with encouraging analogies and attractive, doubtful eggs called possibilities. Will clearly saw the pitiable cases of prolonged incubation that hatched nothing. Had gratitude not restrained him, he would have laughed at Casaubon, whose plodding industry, rows of notebooks and little candle of learned theory probing the world's scattered ruins seemed to point to a moral entirely favourable to Will's generous trust in the universe's intentions for him. He considered that trust a sign of genius, and certainly it is no sign of its absence. Genius lies neither in conceit nor humility, but in the ability to make or do—not just anything, but something particular. Let him leave for the Continent, then, without our delivering a verdict on his future. Of all errors, prophecy is the most unnecessary.

For now, though, this warning against hasty judgment interests me more with regard to Mr. Casaubon than to his young cousin. If for Dorothea he was merely the occasion that ignited the fine combustible material of her youthful illusions, does that mean the cooler observers who have so far judged him portrayed him fairly? I object to every absolute conclusion, every prejudice derived from Mrs. Cadwallader's scorn for a neighbouring clergyman's supposed greatness of soul, or Sir James Chettam's low opinion of his rival's legs; from Mr. Brooke's failure to extract a companion's ideas, or Celia's criticism of a middle-aged scholar's appearance. I doubt that even the greatest man of his age—if such a solitary superlative ever existed—could escape these unflattering reflections in assorted little mirrors. Even Milton, seeking his portrait in a spoon, must accept a country bumpkin's facial angle. And if Mr. Casaubon's own rhetoric is chilly, that does not prove him incapable of good work or fine feeling. Did not an immortal physicist and decipherer of hieroglyphs write dreadful verse? Have graceful manners and tactful conversation advanced our understanding of the solar system? Suppose we turn from external judgments of a man and ask, with greater interest, what his own consciousness reports about his work and abilities. What obstacles accompany his daily labour? What fading hopes, or more deeply fixed self-deceptions, do the years register within him? In what spirit does he struggle against the universal pressure that will one day grow too heavy and stop his heart? Certainly his fate matters to him. Our main reason for thinking he claims too much of our attention must be that we lack room for him, since we commend him to Divine care with perfect confidence. Indeed, we consider it sublime for our neighbour to expect everything there, however little we have given him ourselves. Mr. Casaubon too stood at the centre of his own world. If he tended to think Providence had made others for him, particularly to assess their suitability for the author of a “Key to all Mythologies,” that trait is not entirely foreign to us. Like mortals' other begging hopes, it deserves some of our pity.

His marriage to Miss Brooke certainly affected him more closely than any of those who had expressed disapproval. At this stage I feel more tenderness towards his experience of success than towards the kindly Sir James's disappointment. In truth, as the wedding approached, Mr. Casaubon's spirits did not rise. Contemplating the garden scene of marriage, where all accounts promised a path bordered with flowers, did not consistently enchant him more than the familiar vaults through which he walked holding his little candle. He did not admit to himself, much less could he have told anyone else, his surprise that in winning a lovely, noble-hearted girl he had failed to win delight. Delight too he had considered something that could be found by searching. True, he knew every classical passage saying otherwise.
