But knowledge of classical passages, we find, is a form of motion, which explains why so little surplus energy remains for applying them personally.

Poor Mr. Casaubon had imagined his long, studious bachelorhood had earned him compound interest in enjoyment, and that large withdrawals from his affections would be duly honoured. All of us, serious or frivolous, entangle our thoughts in metaphors and act disastrously on their authority. Now the very certainty that his circumstances were unusually happy threatened to sadden him. No external cause explained the emotional blankness that overcame him precisely when joyful expectation should have been strongest, when he exchanged his dull Lowick library for visits to the Grange. This wearying experience condemned him to a loneliness as complete as the despair that sometimes threatened while he struggled in authorship's swamp, seemingly no nearer his goal. His was the worst loneliness, the kind that shrinks from sympathy. He could not help wanting Dorothea to think him as happy as the world expected her successful suitor to be. As an author, he leaned upon her youthful trust and reverence. Drawing out her fresh interest as a listener encouraged him. In speaking to her, he presented his achievements and intentions with a teacher's reflected confidence, temporarily dismissing that chilling imaginary audience whose ghostly pressure of Tartarean shades crowded his laborious, uncreative hours.

For Dorothea, after the toy-box world history adapted for young ladies that had formed most of her education, his talk about the great book opened new vistas. The sense of revelation, the surprise of meeting Stoics and Alexandrians more closely as people with ideas not entirely unlike her own, temporarily suspended her usual eagerness for a unifying theory. Such a theory would bind her life and beliefs firmly to that astonishing past and connect the remotest sources of knowledge with her actions. Fuller teaching would follow; Mr. Casaubon would explain it all. She anticipated a higher initiation into ideas as she anticipated marriage, blending her hazy conceptions of the two. It would be a great mistake to suppose she wanted a share of his learning merely as an accomplishment. Though Freshitt and Tipton called her clever, that word would not have described her in circles whose more precise vocabulary used cleverness to mean simple aptitude for learning and doing, separate from character. Every wish to learn flowed within the strong current of sympathy that habitually carried her ideas and impulses. She did not want to decorate herself with knowledge, to wear it disconnected from the nerves and blood that nourished her actions. Had she written a book, she would have needed, like Saint Theresa, an authoritative command binding her conscience. Yet she longed for something to fill her life with activity both rational and passionate. Since the time of guiding visions and spiritual directors had passed, since prayer increased longing but supplied no instruction, what lamp remained except knowledge? Surely learned men possessed the only oil. And who was more learned than Mr. Casaubon?

So throughout these short weeks, Dorothea's joyful, grateful expectation remained uninterrupted. However flat her lover might occasionally feel, he could never attribute it to any decline in her loving interest.
The mild season encouraged them to plan a wedding journey extending to Rome. Mr. Casaubon particularly wanted this, because he hoped to examine manuscripts in the Vatican.

“I still regret that your sister will not be coming with us,” he said one morning, some time after it was clear that Celia did not want to go and Dorothea did not want her company. “You will have many solitary hours, Dorothea. I must make the fullest use of our time in Rome, and I would feel freer if you had a companion.”
“I would feel freer” grated on Dorothea. For the first time while speaking to Mr. Casaubon, she blushed with irritation.
“You must have misunderstood me badly,” she said, “if you think I wouldn't appreciate the value of your time, or willingly give up anything that prevented you using it as well as possible.”

“That is very kind of you, my dear Dorothea,” he answered, entirely unaware that she was hurt. “But with a lady companion I could place you both in a guide's care, and we could accomplish two purposes in the same amount of time.”

“Please don't bring this up again,” Dorothea said rather haughtily. Immediately afraid she was wrong, she turned and laid her hand on his, adding in a different voice, “Please don't worry about me. I'll have so much to think about when I'm alone. Tantripp will be companion enough, simply to look after me. I couldn't bear to bring Celia; she'd be miserable.”

It was time to dress. That day brought the last of the Grange's dinner parties considered proper preliminaries to the wedding. At the bell, Dorothea welcomed a reason to leave immediately, as though she needed longer than usual to prepare. She felt ashamed of an irritation whose cause she could not define even to herself. Although she had not meant to be untruthful, her reply had not expressed the real hurt. His words were perfectly reasonable, yet they had instantly conveyed a vague feeling of distance on his part.
“I must be in a strangely weak, selfish state,” she told herself. “How can I have a husband so far above me without recognizing that he needs me less than I need him?”

Once she persuaded herself that he was entirely right, her composure returned. She entered the drawing room in her silver-grey dress, a pleasing image of serene dignity. Her dark brown hair, simply parted above her forehead and heavily coiled behind, matched the complete absence from her manner and expression of any attempt to create an effect. Sometimes in company Dorothea seemed as perfectly at rest as a painting of Santa Barbara looking from her tower into clear air. These quiet intervals only made the energy of her speech and feelings more noticeable when something external stirred her.

Naturally she attracted much comment that evening. The party was large, and its male guests more varied than at any Grange gathering since the nieces had moved in. Conversations took place in pairs and threes of greater or lesser harmony. Middlemarch's newly elected mayor was there, a manufacturer, along with his brother-in-law, a philanthropic banker whose influence in town was so strong that some called him a Methodist and others a hypocrite, depending on their vocabulary. Several professional men attended too. Indeed, Mrs. Cadwallader said Brooke was beginning to entertain the Middlemarch people for political purposes, and she preferred the farmers at the tithe dinner, who drank her health without pretensions and felt no shame about their grandfathers' furniture. In that region, before Reform had notably awakened political consciousness, distinctions of rank were clearer than distinctions of party. Mr. Brooke's assorted invitations therefore seemed part of the general laxity caused by excessive travel and a habit of taking in too many ideas.
Even as Miss Brooke left the dining room, opportunities arose for a few brief “asides.”

“A fine woman, Miss Brooke! An exceptionally fine woman, by God!” said old Mr. Standish, the lawyer. Long association with the landed gentry had made him a landowner himself. He pronounced that oath in a deep voice like a coat of arms, marking the speech of a man of standing.

Mr. Bulstrode, the banker, appeared to be addressed, but disliking coarse language and profanity, he merely bowed. Mr. Chichely took up the remark. A middle-aged bachelor famous in hare coursing, he had a complexion rather like an Easter egg, a few carefully placed hairs and a bearing that suggested awareness of his distinguished appearance.

“Yes, but she isn't my kind of woman. I prefer one who makes a little more effort to please us. A woman ought to have a touch of filigree, something flirtatious. A man enjoys a sort of challenge. The more determinedly she sets her sights on you, the better.”
“There's truth in that,” Mr. Standish said, inclined to be agreeable. “And by God, it's usually their way. I suppose it serves some wise purpose. Providence made them so, eh, Bulstrode?”
“I would be inclined to trace flirtatiousness to a different source,” Mr. Bulstrode replied. “I would attribute it to the devil.”

“Yes, certainly, a woman should have a little devil in her,” said Mr. Chichely, whose study of the fair sex seemed to have injured his theology. “And I like them fair, with a particular walk and a swan's neck. Between ourselves, the mayor's daughter suits me better than either Miss Brooke or Miss Celia. If I intended to marry, I'd choose Miss Vincy over either of them.”
“Well then, make your move,” Mr. Standish joked. “You can see it's the middle-aged men who win the day.”
Mr. Chichely shook his head meaningfully. He was not about to expose himself to the certainty of acceptance by his chosen woman.

The Miss Vincy honoured as Mr. Chichely's ideal was, of course, absent. Mr. Brooke, always opposed to going too far, would not have wanted his nieces to meet a Middlemarch manufacturer's daughter except at a public event. None of the women present could offend Lady Chettam or Mrs. Cadwallader. Mrs. Renfrew, the colonel's widow, was beyond criticism in breeding, and interesting besides for an ailment that baffled the doctors. It plainly seemed a case where the fullest professional knowledge might need quackery's assistance. Lady Chettam attributed her own excellent health to homemade bitters combined with constant medical supervision. She imaginatively entered into Mrs. Renfrew's description of her symptoms and the astonishing uselessness of every strengthening medicine.
“Where can all the strength in those medicines be going, my dear?” the gentle but dignified dowager asked Mrs. Cadwallader thoughtfully when Mrs. Renfrew's attention turned elsewhere.

“It strengthens the illness,” replied the Rector's wife, much too well-born not to practise amateur medicine. “Everything depends on the constitution. Some people produce fat, some blood, some bile—that's how I see it. Whatever they take is so much grist for their mill.”
“Then she should take medicines that reduce things—reduce the illness, you know, if you're right, my dear. And I do think what you say makes sense.”
“Of course it makes sense. Take two kinds of potato grown in the same soil. One becomes more and more watery—”

“Ah! Like poor Mrs. Renfrew. That's exactly what I think. Dropsy! There's no swelling yet because it's internal. I'd say she needs drying medicines, wouldn't you? Or a dry hot-air bath. One could try all sorts of drying treatments.”
“Let her try a certain person's pamphlets,” Mrs. Cadwallader murmured as the gentlemen entered. “He has no need of drying out.”
“Who, my dear?” asked Lady Chettam, a charming woman whose quickness never spoiled the pleasure of explaining.
“The bridegroom, Casaubon. He's certainly dried up faster since the engagement. The fire of passion, I suppose.”
“I would think his constitution far from sound,” Lady Chettam said even more softly. “And then those studies of his—so very dry, as you say.”

“Really, beside Sir James he looks like a skull covered in skin for the occasion. Mark my words: a year from now that girl will hate him. She worships him as an oracle today; soon she'll go to the opposite extreme. Sheer flightiness!”
“How shocking! I'm afraid she's headstrong. But tell me—you know all about him—is something seriously wrong? What's the truth?”
“The truth? He's as bad as the wrong medicine: unpleasant to swallow, certain to upset you.”

“Nothing could be worse,” Lady Chettam said. Her conception of the medicine was so vivid that she seemed to have learned something precise about Mr. Casaubon's defects. “Still, James won't hear a word against Miss Brooke. He continues to call her the model of womanhood.”
“That's generous pretence. Depend on it, he likes little Celia better, and she appreciates him. I hope you're fond of my little Celia?”

“Certainly. She likes geraniums more, and seems more compliant, though her figure isn't so fine. But we were discussing medicine. Tell me about this young surgeon, Mr. Lydgate. They say he's wonderfully clever. He certainly looks it—a very fine forehead.”
“He's a gentleman. I heard him speaking with Humphrey. He expresses himself well.”

“Yes. Mr. Brooke says he belongs to the Northumberland Lydgates, really good connections. One doesn't expect that in such a practitioner. Personally, I prefer a medical man nearer the servants' level; they're often all the cleverer. Poor Hicks's judgment never failed me, I assure you. I never knew him to be wrong. Coarse, like a butcher, but he understood my constitution. His sudden death was a real loss to me. Goodness, how animatedly Miss Brooke seems to be talking with this Mr. Lydgate!”
“She's discussing cottages and hospitals,” Mrs. Cadwallader said, quick both to hear and interpret. “I believe he's a kind of philanthropist, so Brooke is bound to take an interest in him.”
“James,” Lady Chettam said when her son approached, “bring Mr. Lydgate over and introduce us. I want to test him.”
The friendly dowager professed delight at the chance to meet Mr. Lydgate, having heard how successfully he treated fever by a new method.

Mr. Lydgate possessed the medical skill of looking perfectly serious no matter what nonsense he heard. His steady dark eyes made him an impressive listener. He resembled the lamented Hicks as little as possible, particularly in a certain effortless refinement of dress and speech. Even so, Lady Chettam developed considerable confidence in him. By conceding that every constitution could be called peculiar, he confirmed her opinion of her own; and he did not deny that hers might be more peculiar than most. He disapproved of excessively weakening treatments, including indiscriminate cupping, but equally of endless port wine and medicinal bark. He said “I think so” with such deference accompanying the insight of his agreement that she formed the warmest opinion of his abilities.
“I'm very pleased with your protégé,” she told Mr. Brooke before leaving.
“My protégé? Goodness me! Who do you mean?” Mr. Brooke asked.
“Young Lydgate, the new doctor. He strikes me as understanding his profession admirably.”

“Oh, Lydgate! He's not my protégé, you know. I simply knew an uncle of his who wrote to me about him. Still, I think he'll prove first-rate. Studied in Paris, knew Broussais, has ideas, you know. Wants to improve the profession.”
“Lydgate has plenty of entirely new ideas about ventilation and diet and so forth,” Mr. Brooke resumed after seeing Lady Chettam out and returning to entertain a group of Middlemarch men.
“Hang it, is that really sound?” Mr. Standish asked. “Overturning the old treatments that have made Englishmen what they are?”

“Medical knowledge among us is at a low level,” Mr. Bulstrode said in his subdued voice, looking rather sickly. “For my part, I welcome Mr. Lydgate's arrival. I hope to find good grounds for placing the new hospital under his direction.”

“Very fine,” retorted Mr. Standish, who disliked Mr. Bulstrode. “If you want him experimenting on your hospital patients and killing a few people for charity, I've no objection. But I won't pay out of my own pocket to be experimented on. I prefer a treatment that's had a little testing.”
“Well, Standish, you know every dose you swallow is an experiment—an experiment, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, nodding at the lawyer.
“Oh, if that's what you mean!” Mr. Standish replied, displaying as much disgust at such non-legal quibbling as a man could decently show a valuable client.

“I'd welcome any treatment that cured me without leaving me a skeleton like poor Grainger,” said Mr. Vincy, the mayor. His ruddy flesh would have made a striking painter's study beside Mr. Bulstrode's Franciscan colouring. “It's extraordinarily dangerous to be left with no padding against the arrows of disease, as somebody said—and I think it's a very good phrase myself.”

Mr. Lydgate was, of course, beyond earshot. He had left early and would have found the party wholly tedious except for the novelty of meeting certain people. Miss Brooke especially interested him: her youthful freshness, forthcoming marriage to that faded scholar, and interest in socially useful matters formed an unusual, intriguing combination.

“A good creature, that handsome girl, but rather too earnest,” he thought. “Talking to women like that is troublesome. They always want reasons, yet know too little to understand the merits of a question, and usually fall back on their moral sense to settle it according to their own tastes.”

Clearly Miss Brooke was no more Mr. Lydgate's kind of woman than Mr. Chichely's. For the latter, whose mind was fully mature, she was an outright mistake, liable to shake his faith in final causes—including the purpose of fine young women being suited to purple-faced bachelors. Lydgate, however, was less fully ripened. Experience might yet alter his view of a woman's finest qualities.
Neither gentleman, however, saw Miss Brooke again under her maiden name. Shortly after that dinner party she became Mrs. Casaubon and set out for Rome.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter XI
paragraphs:
But actions and speech of the kind people use,
And characters comedy herself would choose
To hold up an image of life in our times,
And play with our follies instead of our crimes.
—BEN JONSON.

Lydgate already knew, in fact, that a woman strikingly unlike Miss Brooke fascinated him. He did not remotely imagine he had lost his balance and fallen in love, but he had said of this woman, “She is grace itself, completely lovely and accomplished. That's what a woman ought to be. She should affect you like exquisite music.” He viewed plain women as he did life's other harsh facts: things to be faced philosophically and investigated scientifically. Rosamond Vincy, however, seemed to possess the true charm of melody. And once a man has seen the woman he would choose if he intended to marry soon, his continued bachelorhood usually depends more on her resolve than his. Lydgate believed he would remain unmarried for several years, until he had beaten out a clear path for himself away from the broad, ready-made road. Miss Vincy had been visible above his horizon almost as long as Mr. Casaubon had taken to become engaged and married. But that learned gentleman had a fortune, had amassed his extensive notes, and had acquired the kind of reputation that precedes achievement—often the larger share of a man's fame. As we have seen, he took a wife to adorn the remaining quarter of his course, a little moon whose effect on his orbit would be barely measurable. Lydgate, however, was young, poor and ambitious. His half-century lay ahead, not behind, and he had come to Middlemarch determined to do many things unlikely to make his fortune or even guarantee a good income. For a man in such circumstances, acquiring a wife is more than a matter of adornment, however highly he values it; Lydgate was inclined to rank adornment first among a wife's functions. Guided by a single conversation, he thought this was where Miss Brooke would fall short, despite her undeniable beauty. She did not see things from the proper feminine angle. The company of such women was about as relaxing as leaving work to teach a class of schoolboys, instead of reclining in paradise with sweet laughter for birdsong and blue eyes for heaven.

At present few things could seem less important to Lydgate than Miss Brooke's cast of mind, or to Miss Brooke than the qualities of the woman attracting this young surgeon. Yet anyone watching closely as human destinies quietly converge sees one life's effects on another slowly taking shape. They cast a calculated irony on the indifference or icy stare we direct at a neighbour we have not met. Destiny stands by, sarcastic, holding our folded cast list.

Old provincial society had its share of this subtle motion. It had not only spectacular downfalls, brilliant young professional dandies ending up in an alley with a slovenly woman and six children as their household, but also less conspicuous changes that continually shifted the boundaries of social contact and created new awareness of mutual dependence. Some slipped a little lower, others found a higher foothold. People who dropped their h's gained fortunes, and fastidious gentlemen stood for borough seats. Some were swept into political currents, others into church disputes, and found themselves in surprising company. A few people or families stood rock-solid amid the changes, yet even they slowly showed new aspects, altered both by changes in themselves and in those observing them. Town and country parish gradually spun new connecting threads, as money left the old stocking for the savings bank and worship of the golden guinea died away. Squires, baronets, even lords, once living blamelessly remote from the townspeople's awareness, acquired the defects exposed by closer acquaintance. Newcomers arrived from distant counties, some with alarmingly novel skills, others with offensively superior cunning. Much the same movement and mingling occurred in old England as we find in the older Herodotus, who also thought it well to begin his account of the past with a woman's fate. Io, apparently lured as a girl by attractive merchandise, was the opposite of Miss Brooke. In that respect she perhaps resembled Rosamond Vincy more closely. Rosamond had excellent taste in clothes, with the nymphlike figure and pure fairness that allow the widest choice of fabric's flow and colour. These were only part of her charm. Everyone acknowledged her as the flower of Mrs. Lemon's school, the county's leading establishment, where teaching covered every requirement for an accomplished woman, including extras such as entering and leaving a carriage. Mrs. Lemon herself always held Miss Vincy up as an example: no pupil surpassed her in acquired knowledge or correct speech, and her musical performance was exceptional. We cannot control how people describe us. Had Mrs. Lemon described Juliet or Imogen, those heroines probably would not have sounded poetic either. For most observers, one glimpse of Rosamond would have dispelled any prejudice aroused by such praise.

Lydgate could not remain long in Middlemarch without enjoying that sight, or indeed meeting the Vincys. Mr. Peacock, whose practice he had paid to enter, had not been their doctor—Mrs. Vincy disliked his weakening treatments—but many of their friends and relations had been his patients. Who of any consequence in Middlemarch was not related to, or at least acquainted with, the Vincys? They were established manufacturers and had kept a prosperous household for three generations, naturally intermarrying often with neighbours of varying degrees of gentility. Mr. Vincy's sister had married money in accepting Mr. Bulstrode. Yet as an outsider of obscure origin, Bulstrode was thought fortunate to connect himself with a genuine Middlemarch family. Mr. Vincy, on the other hand, had stepped down a little by marrying an innkeeper's daughter. Even here, though, money offered encouragement. Mrs. Vincy's sister had been rich old Mr. Featherstone's second wife and had died childless years before, leaving nephews and nieces who might be supposed to hold a place in the widower's affections. It happened that Bulstrode and Featherstone, two of Peacock's most important patients, had for different reasons warmly welcomed his successor. Lydgate had already provoked both discussion and partisanship. Mr. Wrench, the Vincys' doctor, soon found reason to think poorly of his professional discretion, and every report about him reached the frequently visited Vincy home. Mr. Vincy preferred general friendliness to taking sides, but had no need to rush into acquaintance with any newcomer. Rosamond silently wished her father would invite Mr. Lydgate. She was tired of familiar faces and figures, the assorted irregular profiles, walks and turns of phrase belonging to Middlemarch young men she had known as boys. At school she had mixed with higher-ranking girls whose brothers, she was certain, could have interested her more than these unavoidable local companions. But she would not have chosen to tell her father her wish, and he felt no urgency himself. An alderman about to become mayor would eventually need larger dinner parties, but for now his well-provided table had plenty of guests.

That table often remained covered with breakfast remnants long after Mr. Vincy and his second son had gone to the warehouse, and Miss Morgan was well into morning lessons with the younger girls in the schoolroom. It waited for the family's late riser, who found any inconvenience to others preferable to getting up when called. So it was one morning that October, when we have lately seen Mr. Casaubon visiting the Grange. Though the fire had overheated the room enough to send the spaniel panting to a distant corner, Rosamond for some reason stayed over her embroidery longer than usual. Occasionally she gave a small shake and rested the work on her knee, studying it with hesitant weariness. Her mother, back from a visit to the kitchen, sat across the little worktable in more complete contentment. Then the clock warned that it was about to strike again, and she looked up from the lace her plump fingers were mending and rang the bell.
“Knock on Mr. Fred's door again, Pritchard, and tell him it's half past ten.”

She spoke without altering the radiant good humour of a face into which forty-five years had carved neither angles nor parallel lines. Pushing back her pink cap ribbons, she rested her work in her lap and gazed admiringly at her daughter.
“Mamma,” Rosamond said, “when Fred comes down, please don't let him have smoked herrings. I can't bear their smell all through the house at this time of morning.”
“Oh, my dear, you're so hard on your brothers! It's the only fault I find in you. Nobody has a sweeter temper, but you're so touchy with your brothers.”
“Not touchy, mamma. You never hear me speak in an unladylike manner.”
“But you do want to keep things from them.”
“Brothers can be so disagreeable.”
“Oh, my dear, you must make allowances for young men. Be grateful if they have good hearts. A woman must learn to tolerate little things. You'll marry one day.”
“Certainly not someone who resembles Fred.”

“Don't disparage your own brother, dear. Few young men have so little against them, even if he couldn't get his degree. I can't understand why; he seems wonderfully clever to me. You know they considered him fit for the best company at college. Particular as you are, I'm surprised you aren't pleased to have such a gentlemanly brother. You're always faulting Bob for not being Fred.”
“Oh no, mamma. Only for being Bob himself.”
“Well, dear, you won't find any young man in Middlemarch who has nothing against him.”
“But”—Rosamond smiled, suddenly revealing two dimples. She did not like these dimples herself and seldom smiled in general company. “But I don't intend to marry a young man from Middlemarch.”
“So it seems, my love, since you've practically refused the pick of them. If there's someone better to be had, I'm sure no girl deserves him more.”
“Forgive me, mamma, but I wish you wouldn't say ‘the pick of them.’”
“Why, what else should I call them?”
“I mean, mamma, that it's a rather vulgar phrase.”
“Very likely, dear. I've never spoken particularly well. What ought I to say?”
“You could say ‘the best of them.’”
“That sounds just as plain and ordinary. With time to think, I'd have said ‘the most superior young men.’ But with your education, you must know.”

“What must Rosy know, mother?” Mr. Fred asked. While the women bent over their work, he had slipped unnoticed through the half-open door. Now he stood with his back to the fire, warming the bottoms of his slippers.
“Whether ‘superior young men’ is the right expression,” Mrs. Vincy replied, ringing the bell.
“Oh, everything's superior tea and superior sugar now. ‘Superior’ is becoming shopkeepers' slang.”
“Have you started to dislike slang, then?” Rosamond asked with gentle seriousness.
“Only the wrong kind. Every choice of words is slang. It identifies a class.”
“Correct English exists, and it isn't slang.”
“Excuse me: correct English is the slang of the prigs who write histories and essays. And the most extreme slang of all belongs to poets.”
“You'll say anything to win an argument, Fred.”
“Then tell me: is it slang or poetry to call an ox a _leg-plaiter_?”
“You're free to call it poetry if you choose.”
“Aha, Miss Rosy, you can't tell Homer from slang. I'll invent a game: write scraps of slang and poetry on slips of paper and ask you to sort them.”
“Dear me, how entertaining young people's conversation is!” Mrs. Vincy said with cheerful admiration.

“Nothing else for my breakfast, Pritchard?” Fred asked the servant bringing coffee and buttered toast. He walked round the table inspecting the ham, potted beef and other cold leftovers with an air of silent rejection, politely refraining from visible disgust.
“Would you care for eggs, sir?”
“Eggs? No! Get me a grilled bone.”

“Really, Fred,” Rosamond said once the servant had gone, “if you need hot food for breakfast, I wish you'd come down earlier. You can rise at six for hunting. I don't understand why it's so hard on other mornings.”
“That's your failure to understand, Rosy. I get up for hunting because I enjoy it.”
“What would you think if I appeared two hours after everyone else and ordered a grilled bone?”
“I'd think you an exceptionally fast young lady,” Fred answered, eating his toast with perfect calm.
“I don't see why brothers should be allowed to make themselves unpleasant any more than sisters.”
“I don’t make myself unpleasant; you are the one who finds me unpleasant. That word describes your feelings, not anything I do.”
“I think it describes the smell of a grilled bone.”

“Not at all. It describes something in your little nose connected with certain fussy notions that form the classics of Mrs. Lemon's school. Look at mother. She doesn't object to everything she doesn't do herself. She's my idea of an agreeable woman.”
“Bless you both, my dears. Don't quarrel,” Mrs. Vincy said with motherly warmth. “Now, Fred, tell us about the new doctor. How does your uncle like him?”
“Quite well, I think. He asks Lydgate every sort of question, then screws up his face at the answers as if they were pinching his toes. That's his way. Ah, here's my grilled bone.”
“But why were you out so late, dear? You only said you were visiting your uncle.”
“Oh, I had dinner at Plymdale's. We played whist. Lydgate was there as well.”
“And what do you think of him? Very gentlemanly, I imagine. They say his family's excellent, his relations proper county people.”
“Yes,” Fred said. “There was a Lydgate at John's who spent unlimited money. It turns out this fellow's his second cousin. But a rich man may have some very poor devils as second cousins.”

“Good family always makes a difference, though,” Rosamond said with the firmness of someone who had considered the subject. She felt she might have been happier if her father had not been a Middlemarch manufacturer. Anything recalling her mother's father as an innkeeper annoyed her. Certainly someone remembering that fact might think Mrs. Vincy looked like a very handsome, cheerful landlady, accustomed to gentlemen's most capricious demands.
“I thought Tertius was an odd name,” her bright-faced mother said, “but of course it must run in the family. Now, tell us exactly what he's like.”
“Oh, fairly tall, dark, clever, a good talker. Rather a prig, I'd say.”
“I never understand what you mean when you say ‘prig,’” Rosamond said.
“Someone keen to show you he has opinions.”
“But dear, doctors have to have opinions,” Mrs. Vincy said. “What else are they for?”
“Yes, mother, the opinions we pay them for. A prig is someone forever giving you his opinions as a present.”
“I imagine Mary Garth admires Mr. Lydgate,” Rosamond remarked, with a trace of insinuation.

“Really, I couldn't say,” Fred answered rather gloomily. He left the table, picked up the novel he had brought downstairs and dropped into an armchair. “If you're jealous, go to Stone Court more often yourself and outshine her.”
“I wish you wouldn't be so vulgar, Fred. If you've finished eating, please ring the bell.”

“Still, what your brother says is true, Rosamond,” Mrs. Vincy began after the table was cleared. “It's a thousand pities you can't find the patience to visit your uncle more. He's so proud of you, and wanted you to live with him. Who knows what he might have done for you as well as Fred? God knows I love having you at home, but I can part with my children for their own good. And now of course your uncle Featherstone will do something for Mary Garth.”

“Mary Garth can endure Stone Court because she prefers it to being a governess,” Rosamond replied, folding her work. “I'd rather inherit nothing if I had to earn it by putting up with much of my uncle's coughing and his ugly relations.”

“He can't have long left, dear. I wouldn't hurry his end, but between the asthma and that internal complaint, we must hope the next world has something better for him. I bear Mary Garth no ill will, but justice matters too. Mr. Featherstone's first wife brought him no money, unlike my sister. Her nieces and nephews can't have as strong a claim as my sister's. And I must say Mary Garth is a dreadfully plain girl, better suited to being a governess.”
“Not everyone would agree with you about that, mother,” said Fred, apparently able to listen and read simultaneously.

“Well, my dear,” Mrs. Vincy said, deftly changing direction, “even if she _were_ left some money, a man marries his wife's relations, and the Garths are terribly poor and live in such a small way. But I'll leave you to study, dear. I must do some shopping.”
“Fred's studies aren't particularly deep,” Rosamond said, rising with her mother. “He's only got a novel.”

“Well, well, he'll turn to his Latin and so on later,” Mrs. Vincy soothed, stroking his head. “They've lit a fire specially in the smoking room. You know it's what your father wants, Fred, dear, and I always tell him you'll be good and return to college for your degree.”
Fred drew his mother's hand down and kissed it, without answering.
“I suppose you're not planning to ride today?” Rosamond asked, staying behind briefly after her mother left.
“No. Why do you ask?”
“Papa says I'm allowed to ride the chestnut now.”
“Come with me tomorrow if you like. Only remember, I'm going to Stone Court.”
“I'm so eager to ride that I don't mind where we go.” In truth, Stone Court was exactly where Rosamond wanted to go.
“Oh, Rosy,” Fred called as she was leaving, “if you're going to the piano, let me come and play a few tunes with you.”
“Please don't ask me to do that this morning.”
“Why should this morning be different?”
“Really, Fred, I wish you'd stop playing the flute. A man looks so foolish with one. And you play terribly out of tune.”
“Next time someone courts you, Miss Rosamond, I'll let him know how obliging you are.”
“Why should you expect me to oblige you by listening to your flute any more than I should expect you to oblige me by leaving it alone?”
“Then why should you expect me to take you riding?”
This question brought about a compromise, since Rosamond was determined on that particular ride.

So Fred enjoyed nearly an hour practising “Ar hyd y nos,” “Ye banks and braes” and other favourite tunes from his “Instructor on the Flute.” His wheezy performance carried great ambition and an irrepressible hope of better things.

chapters.title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter XII
paragraphs:
He had more fibre on his spinning staff
Than Gerveis knew.
—CHAUCER.

The next morning Fred and Rosamond rode to Stone Court through a pretty stretch of Midlands countryside, nearly all meadow and pasture. The hedges were still allowed to grow in bushy beauty, spreading coral-coloured fruit for the birds. Small details gave each field a distinct face, beloved by eyes that had known it since childhood: the pool in the corner, with wet grass and trees leaning as though to whisper; the great oak shading a bare patch in the middle of the pasture; the high bank topped with ash trees; the abrupt slope of an old marl pit, red behind the burdock; the crowded roofs and hayricks of a farmstead with no visible approach; the grey gate and fences against the bordering wood's depths; and an isolated shed, its ancient thatch full of mossy hills and hollows, wonderfully varied by light and shade. We travel far to see such things later in life and find them grander, but not more beautiful. These are the notes that compose the full scale of landscape joy for souls bred in the Midlands: the things they toddled among, or learned by heart while standing between their father's knees as he drove at leisure.

The road, even the byroad, was excellent. As we have seen, Lowick was no parish of muddy lanes and impoverished tenants, and after two miles Fred and Rosamond entered it. Another mile would take them to Stone Court. Halfway along, the house came into view, looking as though its growth into a stone mansion had been arrested by an unexpected outbreak of farm buildings on its left side, keeping it merely the solid residence of a gentleman farmer. The cluster of pointed corn ricks, balancing the fine walnut row on the right, made it no less pleasing from a distance.
Soon they could distinguish something resembling a gig on the circular drive outside the front door.
“Dear me,” Rosamond said, “I hope none of uncle's dreadful relations are visiting.”

“They are, though. That's Mrs. Waule's gig, the last yellow one left, I'd imagine. Seeing her in it makes me understand how yellow could have been a mourning colour. That gig looks more funereal than a hearse. But Mrs. Waule's always wearing black crape. How does she manage it, Rosy? Her friends can't be dying all the time.”

“I have no idea. And she isn't at all evangelical,” Rosamond reflected, as though that religious outlook would sufficiently explain perpetual mourning crape. After a pause she added, “Or poor, either.”

“No, by George! The Waules and Featherstones are as rich as Jews—I mean for people like them, who want to spend nothing. Yet they hover round my uncle like vultures, terrified a farthing might leave their side of the family. I believe he hates every one of them.”

That very morning Mrs. Waule, so little admired by these distant connections, had happened to say she had no wish “to enjoy their good opinion.” She said it not defiantly but in a low, muffled, neutral voice, as though heard through cotton wool. She was sitting, she observed, at her own brother's hearth. She had been Jane Featherstone for twenty-five years before she was Jane Waule, which entitled her to speak when people with no right to do so took liberties with her brother's name.

“What are you getting at?” Mr. Featherstone asked, holding his stick between his knees and adjusting his wig. He shot her a sharp glance that seemed to recoil on him like a cold draught, setting him coughing.

Mrs. Waule had to wait until he quietened, until Mary Garth supplied fresh syrup and he began rubbing his stick's gold knob, glaring bitterly at the fire. Though bright, the fire did nothing to warm the chilly purple tinge of Mrs. Waule's face, as neutral as her voice, with mere slits for eyes and lips that scarcely moved when she spoke.
“The doctors can't get the better of that cough, brother. It's just like mine. I'm your own sister, constitution and all. But as I was saying, it's a pity Mrs. Vincy's family can't behave better.”
“Tchah! You said nothing of the kind. You said someone had been taking liberties with my name.”

“Nothing that can't be proved, if what everyone says is true. My brother Solomon tells me they're talking all over Middlemarch about young Vincy's unsteadiness, gambling at billiards constantly since he came home.”
“Nonsense! What's wrong with billiards? A good gentlemanly game, and young Vincy isn't a clodhopper. Your son John, now, he'd make a fool of himself if he tried it.”

“Your nephew John has never taken to billiards or any other game, brother. He's far from losing hundreds of pounds, which, if people are right, must come from somewhere other than his father Mr. Vincy's pocket. They say Mr. Vincy's lost money for years, though you'd never guess from his coursing and their open house. And I hear Mr. Bulstrode condemns Mrs. Vincy beyond anything for being so flighty and spoiling her children.”
“What's Bulstrode to me? I don't keep my money with him.”

“Well, Mrs. Bulstrode is Mr. Vincy's own sister, and they say he does most of his business on the bank's money. And you can see for yourself, brother, how unbecoming it is for a woman over forty to have pink ribbons always flying and that frivolous way of laughing at everything. But indulging children is one thing, finding money for their debts another. It's openly said young Vincy has borrowed against his expectations. I don't say what expectations. Miss Garth can hear me and is welcome to repeat it. I know young people stick together.”
“No, thank you, Mrs. Waule,” Mary Garth replied. “I dislike hearing gossip far too much to want to pass it on.”
Mr. Featherstone rubbed his stick's knob and briefly displayed a convulsive laugh, about as genuine as an old whist player's chuckle over a poor hand. Still watching the fire, he said—
“And who's saying Fred Vincy has no expectations? A fine, spirited fellow like him is likely enough to have some.”
Mrs. Waule waited a little before answering, and when she spoke her voice seemed slightly dampened with tears, although her face remained quite dry.

“Whether he does or doesn't, brother, naturally it hurts me and my brother Solomon to hear your name taken liberties with, when your illness might carry you off suddenly. People no more Featherstones than the clown at the fair are openly counting on your property coming to _them_. And me your own sister, Solomon your own brother! If that's how it is, what did the Almighty make families for?” Here she shed tears, but moderately.
“Come on, out with it, Jane!” Mr. Featherstone said, looking at her. “You mean Fred Vincy has got someone to lend him money on what he claims to know about my will, eh?”

“I never said that, brother.” Her voice was dry and steady again. “My brother Solomon told me last night when he called on his way from market to advise me about the old wheat, me being a widow and my John only twenty-three, though as steady as anyone. He heard it from absolutely reliable sources, not just one but several.”
“Rubbish and nonsense! I don't believe a word. Someone's made it all up. Go to the window, missy. I thought I heard a horse. See whether the doctor's coming.”

“Not made up by me, brother, nor Solomon. Whatever else he is—and I don't deny his oddities—he's made his will and divided everything equally among the relations he's friendly with. For my part, I think some deserve more consideration than others at times. But Solomon makes no secret of his intentions.”

“More fool him!” Mr. Featherstone managed to say with some difficulty, before breaking into a severe coughing fit. Mary had to remain beside him, so she could not discover whose horses presently stood stamping on the gravel outside the door.

Before the coughing stopped, Rosamond entered, gracefully holding up her riding skirt. She bowed formally to Mrs. Waule, who stiffly said, “How do you do, miss?” She smiled and nodded silently at Mary, then remained standing until her uncle's cough would let him notice her.
“Heyday, miss!” he said at last. “You've got a fine colour. Where's Fred?”
“Attending to the horses. He'll come in shortly.”
“Sit down, sit down. Mrs. Waule, you'd best be off.”

Even neighbours who called Peter Featherstone an old fox had never accused him of false politeness. His sister was quite accustomed to the peculiar absence of ceremony with which he acknowledged blood relations. Indeed, she herself believed the Almighty's intentions for families included complete freedom from any need to behave pleasantly. She rose slowly, showing no resentment, and said in her usual muffled monotone, “Brother, I hope this new doctor can help you. Solomon says there's great talk of his cleverness. I'm sure I wish you to be spared. Nobody's more ready to nurse you than your own sister and nieces, if you'd only ask. There's Rebecca and Joanna and Elizabeth, you know.”

“Ay, ay, I remember. You'll find I've remembered all of them, dark and ugly as they are. They'll need some money, eh? Never any beauty among our family's women, but the Featherstones have always had money, and the Waules too. Waule had money. A well-off man, Waule. Ay, money's a good egg; if you've some to leave behind, put it in a warm nest. Goodbye, Mrs. Waule.” He tugged both sides of his wig as though to make himself deaf. His sister left, pondering this oracle. Despite her jealousy of the Vincys and Mary Garth, at the very bottom of her shallow thoughts lay the conviction that her brother could never leave his main property outside his blood family. Otherwise why had the Almighty taken both his wives childless, after manganese and other things unexpectedly turning up had made him so rich? Why did Lowick parish church exist, with the Waules and Powderells sharing a pew for generations and the Featherstone pew beside them, if on the Sunday after Peter's death everyone would know the property had left the family? The human mind has never accepted moral chaos. Such an absurd outcome was not, strictly speaking, conceivable. But many things that frighten us are not strictly conceivable.
When Fred entered, the old man looked him over with a particular twinkle. The younger man had often had reason to read it as pride in the pleasing details of his appearance.
“You two young misses clear off,” Mr. Featherstone said. “I want a word with Fred.”

“Come to my room, Rosamond. You won't mind being cold for a little while,” Mary said. They had known each other since childhood and attended the same provincial school, Mary as a pupil apprenticed to teaching. With many shared memories, they enjoyed private conversations. Indeed, such a _tête-à-tête_ was one reason Rosamond had come.

Old Featherstone waited until the door had closed before beginning the conversation. He kept the same twinkling gaze on Fred and performed one of his habitual grimaces, alternately tightening and widening his mouth. When he spoke, his low voice suggested an informer prepared to be bought off rather than an offended elder. He was not a man to feel strong moral indignation, even about offences against himself. Naturally other people wanted to gain an advantage over him; but then, he was a little too cunning for them.
“So, sir, you've been borrowing at ten per cent, promising to pay by mortgaging my land once I'm dead and gone, eh? Giving me another twelve months, say. But I can still change my will.”

Fred flushed. For excellent reasons he had borrowed no money that way. But he knew he had spoken confidently—perhaps more confidently than he quite remembered—about his prospects of inheriting Featherstone's land as a future means of paying current debts.
“I don't know what you mean, sir. I've certainly never borrowed money on anything so insecure. Please explain.”

“No, sir, you're the one to explain. I can change my will yet, let me tell you. My mind's sound. I can work out compound interest in my head and remember every fool's name as well as twenty years ago. What the devil? I'm not eighty yet. I say you must contradict this story.”

“I have contradicted it, sir,” Fred answered with some impatience. He forgot that his uncle did not distinguish the words contradict and disprove, though nobody was less likely to confuse the ideas. Old Featherstone often wondered at the fools who accepted his assertions as evidence. “But I'll contradict it again. The whole story's a stupid lie.”
“Nonsense! You must bring dockiments. It comes from authority.”
“Tell me the source, make him name the person who lent me money, and then I can disprove it.”
“A pretty good source, I'd say: a man who knows most of Middlemarch's business. That fine religious, charitable uncle of yours. Come now!” Featherstone gave his peculiar inward shake of amusement.
“You mean Mr. Bulstrode?”
“Who else would it be, eh?”
“Then this lie has grown out of some sermonizing remark he made about me. Do they claim he actually named whoever lent me the money?”

“If such a man exists, Bulstrode knows him, depend on it. And if you tried to borrow and failed, Bulstrode would know that too. Bring me something in writing from him, saying he doesn't believe you've ever promised to settle your debts out of my land. Come now!”
Mr. Featherstone's face needed its entire range of grimaces to give muscular expression to his silent triumph in the soundness of his faculties.
Fred found himself trapped in a thoroughly distasteful dilemma.

“You must be joking, sir. Mr. Bulstrode believes dozens of untrue things, like anyone else, and he's prejudiced against me. I could easily get him to write that he knows no facts supporting this report, though even that might cause unpleasantness. But I can hardly ask him to put on paper everything he does or doesn't believe about me.” Fred paused, then appealed strategically to his uncle's vanity. “That isn't really something a gentleman asks for.” The result disappointed him.

“Ay, I know what you mean. You'd rather offend me than Bulstrode. And what's he? No land round here that I've ever heard of. A speckilating fellow! He could collapse any day when the devil stops backing him. That's what his religion's about: he wants God Almighty to take over. Nonsense! One thing I understood clearly when I used to go to church was this: God Almighty sticks to land. He promises land, gives land, makes fellows rich in corn and cattle. But you take the other side. You prefer Bulstrode and speckilation to Featherstone and land.”

“I beg your pardon, sir,” Fred said, standing with his back to the fire and beating his boot with his whip. “I like neither Bulstrode nor speculation.” Feeling himself stalemated, he spoke rather sulkily.

“Well, well, clearly you can manage without me,” the old man said, secretly disliking the possibility of any independence from Fred. “You don't want land to make you a squire instead of a starving parson, nor a hundred pounds to help along the way. All the same to me. I can make five codicils if I want and keep my notes as a nest egg. All the same to me.”
Fred reddened again. Featherstone rarely gave him money, and just now losing the immediate prospect of banknotes seemed almost harder than losing the more distant hope of land.
“I'm not ungrateful, sir. I never meant to disregard any kindness you may intend towards me. Quite the opposite.”

“Very good. Prove it, then. Bring me a letter from Bulstrode saying he doesn't believe you've been boasting and promising to pay your debts from my land. Then, if you're in a scrape, we'll see whether I can't help you a bit. Come now! That's a bargain. Here, give me your arm. I'll try a walk round the room.”

Despite his irritation, Fred had enough kindness to pity the unloved, unrespected old man a little. His swollen legs made him look especially wretched when walking. Supporting him, Fred thought he would not like to be old with his body breaking down. He waited patiently, first at the window for the customary remarks about the guinea fowl and weathercock, then at the sparse bookshelves. Their chief glories in dark calf bindings were Josephus, Culpepper, Klopstock's “Messiah” and several volumes of the “Gentleman's Magazine.”
“Read out those book names to me. Come now! You're a college man.”
Fred read the titles aloud.
“What did missy need more books for? Why must you keep bringing them to her?”
“She enjoys them, sir. She's very fond of reading.”

“Too fond by half,” Mr. Featherstone complained. “She wanted to read while sitting with me, but I stopped that. She's got the newspaper to read aloud. Enough for a day, I'd think. I can't stand seeing her read to herself. Mind you don't bring any more books. Do you hear?”
“Yes, sir, I hear you.” Fred had been given this order before and secretly disobeyed it. He meant to disobey again.
“Ring the bell,” Mr. Featherstone ordered. “I want missy to come downstairs.”

Rosamond and Mary had talked faster than the men. Neither thought of sitting. They stood by the dressing table near the window while Rosamond removed her hat, arranged her veil and touched her hair with her fingertips: hair with a child's fairness, neither flax-coloured nor yellow. Mary looked all the plainer standing at an angle between the two nymphs, one inside the mirror and one outside. Their heavenly blue eyes met, deep enough to hold any exquisite meaning an ingenious observer chose to place there, and deep enough to conceal their owner's meanings if those were less exquisite. Only a few Middlemarch children looked fair beside Rosamond, and her riding habit displayed the delicate curves of her slender figure. Most Middlemarch men, except her brothers, considered Miss Vincy the finest girl in the world; some called her an angel. Mary Garth, by contrast, looked like an ordinary sinner. She was brown-complexioned, her dark curls rough and stubborn, her stature short. It would not be true to complete a satisfying contrast by saying she possessed every virtue. Plainness brings its own temptations and vices as surely as beauty. It may pretend sweetness, or, refusing to pretend, display discontent in all its unpleasantness. At any rate, being called an ugly thing beside one's lovely companion usually produces something beyond admiration for the description's accuracy and fitness. At twenty-two, Mary certainly had not reached the perfect good sense and virtue generally prescribed for less fortunate girls, as though these could be obtained in ready-mixed quantities with resignation added to taste. Her shrewdness contained a vein of satirical bitterness, constantly renewed, never entirely submerged except by a strong current of gratitude towards people who did something to make her content instead of telling her she ought to be. Growing womanhood had softened her plainness, a good, human sort familiar among the mothers of our race in every latitude, under more or less becoming head coverings. Rembrandt would have enjoyed painting her, making her broad features look from the canvas with intelligent honesty. Honesty—truthful fairness—was her governing virtue. She neither created illusions nor indulged them for her own benefit, and in a good mood she had enough humour to laugh at herself. When she and Rosamond were both reflected in the mirror, she said with a laugh—
“What a brown patch I look beside you, Rosy! You're a most unflattering companion.”

“Oh no! Nobody thinks about your looks, Mary; you're so sensible and useful. Beauty matters very little, really,” Rosamond said, turning towards Mary, though her eyes strayed to the fresh view of her own neck in the mirror.
“You mean _my_ beauty,” Mary replied rather dryly.
“Poor Mary takes even kindness badly,” Rosamond thought. Aloud she asked, “What have you been doing lately?”
“Me? Oh, managing the house, pouring syrup, pretending to be pleasant and contented, learning to think badly of everyone.”
“What a miserable life it is for you.”
“No,” Mary replied sharply, tossing her head a little. “I think my life is pleasanter than your Miss Morgan's.”
“Yes, but Miss Morgan is so dull, and not young.”
“I suppose she's interesting to herself. And I'm far from sure that everything becomes easier as you get older.”

“No,” Rosamond reflected. “You wonder what people like that do, with no prospects. Of course they have religion to support them. But,” she added, dimpling, “it's quite different for you, Mary. You might have a proposal.”
“Has someone told you he intends to propose to me?”
“Of course not. I mean there's a gentleman who might fall in love with you, seeing you nearly every day.”
The slight change in Mary's face came chiefly from her determination not to let it change.
“Does seeing someone always make people fall in love?” she replied casually. “I'd think it's just as often a reason to detest each other.”
“Not if they're interesting and agreeable. I hear Mr. Lydgate is both.”
“Oh, Mr. Lydgate!” Mary's tone unmistakably fell into indifference. “You want to find out about him,” she added, unwilling to indulge Rosamond's indirect approach.
“Only whether you like him.”
“Liking doesn't come into it yet. I always need a little kindness to kindle liking. I'm not generous enough to like people who speak to me as if they can't see me.”
“Is he that haughty?” Rosamond asked with increased satisfaction. “You know he comes from a good family?”
“No, he didn't offer that as an explanation.”
“Mary! You're the oddest girl. But what does he look like? Describe him to me.”

“How do you describe a man? I can give you a list: heavy eyebrows, dark eyes, straight nose, thick dark hair, large firm white hands, and—let me think—an exquisite cambric handkerchief. But you'll see for yourself. This is about when he visits, you know.”
Rosamond blushed slightly, but said thoughtfully, “I rather like a lofty manner. I can't bear a young man who chatters.”

“I didn't say Mr. Lydgate was haughty. But _il y en a pour tous les goûts_, as little Mamselle used to say. If any girl can pick the particular kind of conceit she fancies, I'd think it would be you, Rosy.”
“Pride isn't conceit. Fred is what I call conceited.”

“I wish nobody said worse of him. He ought to be more careful. Mrs. Waule's been telling uncle how unsteady he is.” A girlish impulse overruled Mary's judgment. The word “unsteady” carried a vague anxiety, and she hoped Rosamond might say something to dispel it. Deliberately, however, she left out Mrs. Waule's more specific insinuation.
“Oh, Fred's horrid!” Rosamond said. Only with Mary would she have permitted herself such an unsuitable word.
“What exactly do you mean by horrid?”
“He's so lazy, he makes papa so angry, and he says he won't become a clergyman.”
“I think Fred is perfectly right about that.”
“How can you say that, Mary? I thought you had more feeling for religion.”
“He isn't suited to being a clergyman.”
“But he ought to be suited.”—“Well, then, he isn't what he ought to be. I know other people in the same position.”
“But nobody approves of them. I wouldn't want to marry a clergyman myself, but there have to be clergymen.”
“That doesn't mean Fred has to become one.”
“But papa has paid for his education with exactly that in mind! And just suppose he doesn’t inherit any fortune at all?”
“I can imagine that perfectly well,” Mary said dryly.
“Then I'm surprised you can defend him,” Rosamond replied, wanting to press the point.
“I'm not defending him,” Mary laughed. “I'd defend any parish against having him as its clergyman.”
“But of course he'd have to be different if he were a clergyman.”
“Yes, he'd be a thorough hypocrite. He isn't that yet.”
“There's no point talking to you, Mary. You always side with Fred.”
“Why shouldn't I?” Mary said, her face lighting. “He'd side with me. He's the only person who takes any trouble to do something kind for me.”
“You make me very uncomfortable, Mary,” Rosamond said in her gravest, gentlest manner. “I wouldn't tell mamma for anything.”
“What wouldn't you tell her?” Mary demanded angrily.
“Please don't fly into a rage, Mary,” Rosamond said as mildly as before.
“If your mother's afraid Fred might propose, tell her I wouldn't marry him if he did. But as far as I know he doesn't intend to. He certainly never has asked me.”
“Mary, you're always so fierce.”
“And you're always so infuriating.”
“Me? What have I done wrong?”
“Oh, faultless people are always the most infuriating. There's the bell. I think we'd better go down.”
“I didn't intend to quarrel,” Rosamond said, putting her hat on.
“Quarrel? Nonsense, we haven't quarrelled. If you can't lose your temper sometimes, what's the point of being friends?”
“Should I repeat what you've told me?”
“Whatever you like. I never say anything I'm afraid to have repeated. But let's go downstairs.”

Mr. Lydgate arrived rather late that morning, but the visitors stayed long enough to see him. Mr. Featherstone asked Rosamond to sing, and after “Home, sweet home,” which she detested, she kindly offered another of his favourites, “Flow on, thou shining river.” This hard-headed old Overreach approved of sentimental songs as a suitable decoration for girls and as inherently fine: sentiment was what songs ought to contain.
Mr. Featherstone was still applauding and assuring missy her voice was clear as a blackbird's when Mr. Lydgate's horse passed the window.

He had expected the usual dreary, disagreeable routine with an elderly patient, one scarcely able to believe medicine would fail to “set him up” if only the doctor were clever enough. Added to his general disbelief in Middlemarch's attractions, this made a doubly effective background for the sight of Rosamond. Old Featherstone hastened to introduce her ostentatiously as his niece, though he had never bothered to describe Mary that way. Lydgate missed nothing of Rosamond's graceful manner: how delicately she deflected the attention the old man's bad taste forced on her, using a quiet seriousness; how she kept her dimples hidden at the wrong moment, then revealed them while speaking with such kind interest to Mary. Lydgate quickly looked at Mary more closely than ever before and saw an adorable kindness in Rosamond's eyes. Mary, however, seemed rather out of temper for some reason.
“Miss Rosy's been singing to me. No objection to that, eh, doctor?” Mr. Featherstone said. “I like it better than your medicines.”

“That's made me forget the time,” Rosamond said, rising for the hat she had removed before singing. Her flowerlike head on its white stem thus showed to perfection above her riding habit. “Fred, we really must leave.”
“Very well,” Fred replied. He had reasons of his own for being out of spirits and wanting to get away.

“Miss Vincy is musical?” Lydgate asked, following her with his eyes. (Every nerve and muscle in Rosamond adjusted to the knowledge that she was watched. She was a natural actress in roles suited to her _physique_. She even performed her own character so well that she did not recognize it precisely as her own.)
“Best in Middlemarch, I'll wager, whoever comes second,” Mr. Featherstone said. “Eh, Fred? Say a word for your sister.”
“I'm afraid I'm disqualified, sir. My evidence wouldn't count for anything.”
“Middlemarch's standards aren't very high, uncle,” Rosamond said with pretty lightness, moving towards her whip some distance away.

Lydgate anticipated her quickly. He reached the whip first and turned to offer it. She bowed and looked at him; naturally he looked at her. Their eyes met with that particular meeting no effort can achieve, like a sudden divine clearing of mist. I think Lydgate grew a little paler, but Rosamond blushed deeply and felt a certain astonishment. After that she truly wanted to leave, and when she shook her uncle's hand she had no idea what foolish thing he was talking about.

Yet this result, which she understood as the mutual impression called falling in love, was exactly what Rosamond had planned. Since that important newcomer arrived in Middlemarch, she had woven a little future requiring a scene like this for its beginning. Strangers, whether shipwrecked and clutching a raft or properly escorted with luggage, have always held a fascination for the maiden mind against which local merit pleads in vain. A stranger was essential to Rosamond's social romance. It had always required a lover and husband from outside Middlemarch, with relations entirely unlike hers; lately, indeed, the design appeared to demand some connection to a baronet. Now that she and the stranger had met, reality proved far more stirring than anticipation. She could not doubt this was her life's great turning point. She interpreted her symptoms as awakening love and found it even more natural that Mr. Lydgate should love her at first sight. Such things happened constantly at balls; why not in morning light, which improved the complexion? Though no older than Mary, Rosamond was accustomed to inspiring love, while remaining indifferent and exactingly critical herself, whether towards a fresh young sprig or a faded bachelor. Here, suddenly, Mr. Lydgate matched her ideal: wholly foreign to Middlemarch, with an air of distinction fitting good family, and connections offering glimpses of that middle-class heaven, rank. He was talented too, which would make enslaving him especially delightful. In fact, he had stirred her nature in an entirely new way, bringing a vivid interest into her life better than any imagined “might-be” she habitually set against reality.

On the ride home, therefore, both brother and sister were absorbed and inclined to silence. Rosamond's foundation had the usual flimsy airiness, but once she assumed it, her imagination built with remarkable realism and detail. Before they had gone a mile, she was far ahead with the clothes and introductions of married life. She had chosen her Middlemarch house and foreseen visits to her husband's well-bred relations elsewhere, whose polished manners she could acquire as thoroughly as her school accomplishments, preparing herself for less definite future elevations. Nothing financial, still less sordid, entered these visions. She cared about what were considered refinements, not the money needed to buy them.

Fred, meanwhile, was troubled by an anxiety even his ready optimism could not immediately quiet. He saw no way to avoid Featherstone's foolish demand without consequences he liked still less than fulfilling it. His father was already angry with him and would be angrier if Fred caused further coolness between their household and the Bulstrodes. Fred also hated the prospect of approaching his uncle Bulstrode. Perhaps after wine he had said many foolish things about Featherstone's property, magnified in the retelling. He felt he cut a miserable figure, boasting about expectations from a strange old miser and begging for certificates on his orders. But those expectations! He really did have them, and surrendering them offered no pleasant alternative. Besides, he had recently incurred a particularly galling debt, which Featherstone had almost agreed to discharge. The whole affair was miserably small. His debts were small; even his expectations were nothing magnificent. Fred had known men to whom he would have been ashamed to admit the small scale of his troubles. Such thoughts naturally produced a streak of bitter dislike for humanity. Born a Middlemarch manufacturer's son, inevitably heir to nothing in particular, while men like Mainwaring and Vyan—certainly life was a poor business if a spirited young fellow with a healthy appetite for the best of everything faced such meagre prospects.

It never occurred to Fred that Featherstone had invented Bulstrode's involvement, nor would knowing it have changed his position. He saw clearly enough that the old man wanted to exercise power by tormenting him, and probably also to enjoy seeing him on uncomfortable terms with Bulstrode. Fred imagined he saw into the depths of his uncle's soul, though half of what he saw was merely the reflection of his own inclinations. Understanding another soul is a difficult task, beyond young gentlemen whose consciousness chiefly consists of their own wishes.

The main question Fred debated with himself was whether to tell his father or try to get through the business without his knowing. Mrs. Waule had probably been gossiping about him. If Mary had repeated her report to Rosamond, it would certainly reach his father, who would just as certainly question him. As they slowed their horses, he asked—
“Rosy, did Mary tell you whether Mrs. Waule had been saying anything about me?”
“Yes, she certainly did.”
“What was it?”
“That you're very unsteady.”
“Was there anything else?”
“I'd have thought that enough, Fred.”
“You're certain she didn't say anything more?”
“Mary didn't mention anything else. But really, Fred, you ought to feel ashamed.”
“Oh, nonsense! Don't lecture me. What did Mary say about it?”
“I don't have to tell you. You care so much about Mary's words, yet you're too rude to let me speak.”
“Of course I care what Mary thinks. She's the best girl I know.”
“I'd never have imagined her the kind of girl someone falls in love with.”
“What do you know about what men fall in love with? Girls never know.”
“At least let me advise _you_ against falling in love with her, Fred. She says she wouldn’t marry you even if you asked.”
“She could have waited until I actually asked her.”
“I knew that would sting you, Fred.”

“Not at all. She wouldn't have said it unless you'd provoked her.” Before they reached home, Fred decided to tell his father the whole story as plainly as possible. Perhaps his father would take on the unpleasant task of speaking to Bulstrode.
